cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: Temporary borrowing does not itself reduce the amount of assets that must eventually be sold; it buys time so that the sales can be conducted in an orderly manner.
cards.explanation: Temporary borrowing is a short-term liquidity buffer. The fund still has to sell assets, but it can do so later and in an orderly way rather than at fire-sale prices.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: In-kind redemption removes the need for the fund to sell the transferred holdings at all, because the assets themselves move to the redeeming investor.
cards.explanation: In-kind redemptions transfer specific securities directly to the redeeming investor, so the fund never has to trade those holdings. It is the one extraordinary measure that genuinely removes the need to sell.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: Swing pricing reduces the incentive to run by shifting trading costs onto the investors who are transacting rather than onto those who remain.
cards.explanation: Swing pricing adjusts NAV when net flows exceed a threshold, so transacting investors bear the trading costs they cause. Remaining shareholders are protected, which weakens the first-mover advantage behind a run.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: A gate eliminates redemption risk over the period it is in force, because outflows above the threshold are cancelled rather than deferred.
cards.explanation: A gate defers redemptions above the threshold to a later date; it does not cancel them. It therefore postpones redemption pressure rather than eliminating redemption risk.
cards.correction: A gate does not eliminate redemption risk over the period it is in force, because outflows above the threshold are deferred rather than cancelled.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: A gate does not eliminate redemption risk over the period it is in force, because outflows above the threshold are deferred rather than cancelled.
cards.explanation: A gate defers redemptions above the threshold to a later date; it does not cancel them. It therefore postpones redemption pressure rather than eliminating redemption risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: Because extraordinary redemption measures are rarely invoked, preparation is best left until a stress event is actually under way, when the relevant facts are known.
cards.explanation: Extraordinary measures are rarely invoked but may be needed on short notice, which is exactly why they must be planned and rehearsed in advance through break-glass testing.
cards.originalText: Because extraordinary measures are rarely invoked, preparation is best left until a stress event is actually under way, when the relevant facts are known.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: In-kind redemption is the most broadly deployable measure, because it can be offered to any investor across any asset type held by the fund.
cards.explanation: In-kind redemption is permitted in both the U.S. and UCITS regimes, but in practice it works only for appropriate asset types and mainly for large institutional investors able to receive securities directly.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: Legal, operations, risk management and trading should conduct break-glass testing of extraordinary redemption measures in advance, so that each measure can be activated on short notice.
cards.explanation: Extraordinary measures are rarely used but may be needed quickly. Advance break-glass testing across legal, operations, risk management and trading ensures they can actually be activated when required.
cards.originalText: Legal, operations, risk management and trading should conduct break-glass testing in advance, so that each measure can be activated on short notice.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed
cards.statement: Because extraordinary redemption measures are regulatory tools, responsibility for activating them rests with the compliance function rather than being a shared operational exercise.
cards.explanation: Activating these measures is a shared operational exercise involving legal, operations, risk management and trading. Compliance alone cannot execute a credit-line drawdown or an in-kind transfer.
cards.originalText: Because these are regulatory tools, responsibility for activating them rests with the compliance function rather than being a shared operational exercise.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difference between risk management and portfolio management, and describe how to use marginal VaR in portfolio management
cards.reading: Reading 87: Jorion, Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods
cards.statement: Marginal VaR is a risk-management output only, because it contains no information about expected returns and therefore cannot inform an allocation decision.
cards.explanation: Marginal VaR contains no return information, but that is why a portfolio manager uses it as the denominator of a return-to-risk ratio. It serves both risk management and portfolio management.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difference between risk management and portfolio management, and describe how to use marginal VaR in portfolio management
cards.reading: Reading 87: Jorion, Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods
cards.statement: Marginal VaR serves both functions, because it is the denominator of the return-to-risk ratio that a portfolio manager equalises across positions and the quantity a risk manager equalises directly.
cards.explanation: A risk manager minimising VaR equalises marginal VaRs across positions, while a portfolio manager equalises expected excess return divided by marginal VaR. The same statistic serves both; only what it is combined with differs.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difference between risk management and portfolio management, and describe how to use marginal VaR in portfolio management
cards.reading: Reading 87: Jorion, Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods
cards.statement: Marginal VaR is a portfolio-management output only, because a risk manager is concerned with total portfolio VaR rather than with the contribution of any individual position.
cards.explanation: Risk managers care a great deal about position-level contributions to risk, which is the purpose of VaR decomposition. Marginal VaR serves both risk management and portfolio management.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difference between risk management and portfolio management, and describe how to use marginal VaR in portfolio management
cards.reading: Reading 87: Jorion, Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods
cards.statement: Marginal VaR informs both functions, and the portfolio manager should act on it by reducing whichever position carries the largest marginal VaR, since that position is the least efficient.
cards.explanation: Cutting the largest marginal VaR is the risk-minimisation rule. A portfolio manager compares marginal VaR against expected excess return; a high marginal VaR signals inefficiency only if the expected return does not keep pace.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: Quality and momentum are style factors.
cards.explanation: Quality and momentum are recognised style factors, alongside value-growth, size, low volatility and carry. They are cross-sectional, dynamically traded strategies with persistent premiums.
cards.originalText: Quality and momentum, as style factors

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: Corporate strategy and brand reputation are style factors.
cards.explanation: Corporate strategy and brand reputation are firm-specific, diversifiable attributes. No risk premium attaches to them and no systematic return series exists, so they are not factors.
cards.originalText: Corporate strategy and brand reputation, as style factors
cards.correction: Corporate strategy and brand reputation are firm-specific attributes.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: Corporate strategy and brand reputation are firm-specific attributes.
cards.explanation: Corporate strategy and brand reputation are firm-specific, diversifiable attributes. No risk premium attaches to them and no systematic return series exists, so they are not factors.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: Economic growth and inflation are macroeconomic factors.
cards.explanation: Economic growth and inflation are the two most standard macroeconomic factors. They are economy-wide states that define bad times for the average investor.
cards.originalText: Economic growth and inflation, as macroeconomic factors

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: Real interest rates and liquidity are macroeconomic factors.
cards.explanation: Real interest rates and liquidity are both listed among the macroeconomic factors, together with economic growth, inflation, volatility, productivity and political risk.
cards.originalText: Real interest rates and liquidity, as macroeconomic factors

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: A factor risk premium is compensation paid to investors for suffering losses during a specific, identifiable set of bad times.
cards.explanation: A factor earns a premium because it delivers poor returns in bad times, when the marginal utility of wealth is high. Investors must be paid to bear those losses.
cards.originalText: Compensation paid to investors for suffering losses during a specific, identifiable set of bad times

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: A factor risk premium is a reward for selecting a set of equities that happens to outperform over a given measurement period.
cards.explanation: Realised outperformance is not a risk premium. A factor premium is an ex-ante expected compensation for a systematic exposure that loses money in bad times, regardless of whether the strategy happened to win.
cards.originalText: A reward for selecting a set of equities that happens to outperform over a given measurement period

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: A factor risk premium is the orthogonal linear combination of variables that maximises the total variance explained.
cards.explanation: That describes a principal component, a statistical factor that maximises explained variance. A principal component has no economic story and need not be priced; a risk premium is compensation for losses in bad times.
cards.originalText: The orthogonal linear combination of variables that maximises the total variance explained
cards.correction: A principal component is the orthogonal linear combination of variables that maximises the total variance explained.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: A principal component is the orthogonal linear combination of variables that maximises the total variance explained.
cards.explanation: That describes a principal component, a statistical factor that maximises explained variance. A principal component has no economic story and need not be priced; a risk premium is compensation for losses in bad times.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: A factor risk premium is the excess return earned by selecting style factors within a single asset class, also known as smart beta.
cards.explanation: Smart beta is an implementation of factor investing within one asset class, not the definition of a premium. A factor risk premium is compensation for bearing losses during bad times.
cards.originalText: The excess return earned by selecting style factors within a single asset class, also known as smart beta

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: Because the value of the bad-times index m is negative, any asset with a non-zero beta with respect to the pricing kernel has a negative expected excess return.
cards.explanation: The pricing kernel m is strictly positive, with E(m) = 1/(1 + Rf). It is the beta with respect to m and the price of bad-times risk that are both negative, and their product gives a positive premium for assets that do badly in bad times.
cards.originalText: Because the value of the bad-times index $m$ is negative, any asset with a non-zero beta with respect to the pricing kernel has a negative expected excess return.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe factors that impact asset prices and explain the theory of factor risk premiums
cards.statement: An increase in an asset's covariance with the bad-times index implies a decrease in the asset's expected return.
cards.explanation: In the pricing-kernel framework both the beta with respect to m and the price of bad-times risk are negative. Raising the covariance (moving it toward zero or above) means the asset does better in bad times, so it acts more like insurance and earns a lower premium.
cards.originalText: An increase in the asset's covariance with the bad-times index, for example from −0.0980 to −0.0270, implies a decrease in the asset's expected return.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: Multifactor asset pricing models price several sources of systematic risk simultaneously, assign a separate beta to each, and like the CAPM assume idiosyncratic risk is diversified away.
cards.explanation: A multifactor model gives each asset one beta per priced factor. Like the CAPM, it treats idiosyncratic risk as diversified away and unpriced; that is a shared feature, not a difference.
cards.originalText: They price several sources of systematic risk simultaneously, assign a separate beta to each, and like the CAPM assume idiosyncratic risk is diversified away.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: Multifactor asset pricing models price several sources of systematic risk simultaneously, but unlike the CAPM they require idiosyncratic risk to be priced as well, since it cannot be diversified away in a multifactor world.
cards.explanation: Adding factors reclassifies some risk from idiosyncratic to systematic, but idiosyncratic risk remains diversified away and unpriced, exactly as in the CAPM.
cards.originalText: They price several sources of systematic risk simultaneously, but unlike the CAPM they require idiosyncratic risk to be priced as well, since it cannot be diversified away in a multifactor world.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: Multifactor asset pricing models replace the market factor entirely, so the market portfolio does not appear on the right-hand side of a multifactor regression.
cards.explanation: Multifactor models usually retain the market factor and add others to it. The Fama-French model, for example, has the market excess return as its first regressor.
cards.originalText: They replace the market factor entirely, so the market portfolio does not appear on the right-hand side of a multifactor regression.
cards.correction: Multifactor asset pricing models usually retain the market factor, so the market portfolio typically appears on the right-hand side of a multifactor regression.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: Multifactor asset pricing models usually retain the market factor, so the market portfolio typically appears on the right-hand side of a multifactor regression.
cards.explanation: Multifactor models usually retain the market factor and add others to it. The Fama-French model, for example, has the market excess return as its first regressor.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: Multifactor asset pricing models assign a single beta measured against a composite of the underlying factors, which is what distinguishes them from the CAPM's single market beta.
cards.explanation: Collapsing factors into one composite beta would just be a single-factor model. Multifactor models assign a separate beta to each factor so exposures can be measured and managed independently.
cards.originalText: They assign a single beta measured against a composite of the underlying factors, which is what distinguishes them from the CAPM's single market beta.
cards.correction: Multifactor asset pricing models assign a separate beta to each of the underlying factors, which is what distinguishes them from the CAPM's single market beta.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: In the CAPM and multifactor models, a high beta to a positively priced factor implies a low risk premium, because a high-beta asset provides a hedge against the factor.
cards.explanation: A high beta to a positively priced factor means the asset co-moves with the factor and loses more when it performs badly, the opposite of a hedge. Such an asset must be compensated with a higher risk premium.
cards.originalText: A high beta implies a low risk premium, because a high-beta asset provides a hedge against the factor.
cards.correction: In the CAPM and multifactor models, a high beta to a positively priced factor implies a high risk premium, because a high-beta asset provides no hedge against the factor.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: In the CAPM and multifactor models, a high beta to a positively priced factor implies a high risk premium, because a high-beta asset provides no hedge against the factor.
cards.explanation: A high beta to a positively priced factor means the asset co-moves with the factor and loses more when it performs badly, the opposite of a hedge. Such an asset must be compensated with a higher risk premium.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: In the CAPM and multifactor models, a high beta to a positively priced factor implies a high risk premium, because a high-beta asset loses more when the factor performs badly and must therefore be compensated.
cards.explanation: Expected excess return equals the sum of factor betas times factor premiums. A high-beta asset falls hard exactly when the factor's bad times arrive, so investors require a higher premium to hold it.
cards.originalText: A high beta implies a high risk premium, because a high-beta asset loses more when the factor performs badly and must therefore be compensated.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM
cards.statement: Beta determines the volatility of the asset but not its risk premium, which is set by idiosyncratic risk.
cards.explanation: Beta measures systematic risk, which is exactly what is priced. Idiosyncratic risk is diversified away and earns no premium.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The market factor, being the excess return on a broad market portfolio, is a factor in the Fama-French three-factor model.
cards.explanation: The Fama-French three-factor model consists of MKT (the market excess return, inherited from the CAPM), SMB (size) and HML (value).
cards.originalText: The market factor, being the excess return on a broad market portfolio

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The difference in expected returns between high-beta stocks and low-beta stocks is a factor in the Fama-French three-factor model.
cards.explanation: A high-beta versus low-beta sort describes the betting-against-beta factor, which comes from a different literature. The Fama-French three factors are MKT, SMB (size) and HML (book-to-market).
cards.originalText: The difference in expected returns between high-beta stocks and low-beta stocks

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The difference in expected returns between a portfolio of high book-to-market stocks and one of low book-to-market stocks is a factor in the Fama-French three-factor model.
cards.explanation: This is HML (high minus low), the value factor in the Fama-French model. A positive HML loading indicates a value tilt and a negative loading a growth tilt.
cards.originalText: The difference in expected returns between a portfolio of high book-to-market stocks and one of low book-to-market stocks

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The difference in expected returns between small-capitalisation stocks and large-capitalisation stocks is a factor in the Fama-French three-factor model.
cards.explanation: This is SMB (small minus big), the size factor in the Fama-French model. A positive SMB loading indicates a small-cap tilt.
cards.originalText: The difference in expected returns between small-capitalisation stocks and large-capitalisation stocks

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The momentum factor, UMD, captures the outperformance of past winners relative to past losers.
cards.explanation: UMD (up minus down, also called WML) sorts stocks on past returns, typically over the prior 12 months skipping the most recent month. It is the fourth factor in the Carhart model, not part of the Fama-French three-factor model.
cards.originalText: The momentum factor, UMD, which captures the outperformance of past winners relative to past losers

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The SMB factor captures the outperformance of high book-to-market firms relative to low book-to-market firms.
cards.explanation: Book-to-market is the value sort, captured by HML. SMB (small minus big) captures the outperformance of small firms relative to large firms.
cards.originalText: The SMB factor, which captures the outperformance of high book-to-market firms relative to low book-to-market firms
cards.correction: The HML factor captures the outperformance of high book-to-market firms relative to low book-to-market firms.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The HML factor captures the outperformance of high book-to-market firms relative to low book-to-market firms.
cards.explanation: Book-to-market is the value sort, captured by HML. SMB (small minus big) captures the outperformance of small firms relative to large firms.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The SMB factor captures the outperformance of small firms relative to large firms.
cards.explanation: SMB (small minus big) sorts on market capitalisation. It is the tradeable expression of the size effect documented by Banz, who found small stocks earned higher beta-adjusted returns.
cards.originalText: The SMB factor, which captures the outperformance of small firms relative to large firms

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example
cards.statement: The momentum factor, UMD, captures the outperformance of high-growth firms relative to low-growth firms.
cards.explanation: Momentum sorts on past returns, capturing past winners minus past losers. Growth stocks are the low book-to-market end of the HML value sort.
cards.originalText: The momentum factor, UMD, which captures the outperformance of high-growth firms relative to low-growth firms

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: Value firms are less flexible and carry more unproductive capital during bad times, so they are riskier when risk matters most.
cards.explanation: This is the standard rational, production-based explanation of the value premium: value firms hold more irreversible capital and adjust poorly when demand falls, so they are more exposed in recessions and the premium compensates that exposure.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: Value stocks generate higher returns during bad economic times, which is what makes them attractive.
cards.explanation: Value stocks do badly in bad times, and that underperformance when risk matters most is the source of the value premium. A strategy that paid off in bad times would be insurance and would earn a low premium.
cards.correction: Value stocks generate lower returns during bad economic times, which is what earns them a premium.

cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: Value stocks generate lower returns during bad economic times, which is what earns them a premium.
cards.explanation: Value stocks do badly in bad times, and that underperformance when risk matters most is the source of the value premium. A strategy that paid off in bad times would be insurance and would earn a low premium.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: Style factors do not persist, because investors eventually discover the factor and trade it away.
cards.explanation: Factor premiums are equilibrium compensation for bearing losses in bad times, so they persist until the underlying economics change. Only a pure mispricing would be arbitraged away.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: Momentum has been the most profitable of the style factors, but momentum strategies exhibit negative skewness.
cards.explanation: Momentum has delivered the highest average return of the value, momentum and size factors, but it pays for it with crash risk: long runs of steady gains punctuated by severe crashes, typically at sharp market reversals.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The opposite of a momentum strategy is portfolio rebalancing, so an investor who rebalances cannot by definition hold the momentum factor.
cards.explanation: Rebalancing is contrarian in mechanics, but that does not rule out momentum exposure. A portfolio can rebalance across asset classes while running a momentum tilt within one.
cards.correction: The opposite of a momentum strategy is portfolio rebalancing, but an investor who rebalances can still hold the momentum factor.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The opposite of a momentum strategy is portfolio rebalancing, but an investor who rebalances can still hold the momentum factor.
cards.explanation: Rebalancing is contrarian in mechanics, but that does not rule out momentum exposure. A portfolio can rebalance across asset classes while running a momentum tilt within one.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The opposite of a momentum strategy is a value strategy, so a factor model containing both contradicts itself or suffers from perfect multicollinearity.
cards.explanation: Value and momentum are negatively correlated, not perfectly collinear. That negative correlation is a reason to hold both, and a factor model can include both without becoming unidentifiable.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The historical value premium is not statistically significant.
cards.explanation: The value premium is statistically significant over long samples and is documented across decades, markets and asset classes. It is one of the headline dynamic style factors.
cards.originalText: No, because the historical value premium is not statistically significant.
cards.correction: The historical value premium is statistically significant.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The historical value premium is statistically significant.
cards.explanation: The value premium is statistically significant over long samples and is documented across decades, markets and asset classes. It is one of the headline dynamic style factors.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The value premium can only be explained by behavioural biases.
cards.explanation: The explanation of the value premium is contested. A rational, risk-based story (value firms are riskier in bad times) competes with behavioural explanations, and both may operate at once.
cards.originalText: Yes, but the value factor can only be explained by behavioural biases.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles
cards.statement: The value premium may be explained by a rational story, by behavioural biases, or by both.
cards.explanation: The value premium is real and expected to persist, but why it exists is unresolved. Rational risk-based and behavioural explanations are both live, and both may operate together.
cards.originalText: Yes, and the value factor may be explained by a rational story, by behavioural biases, or by both.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: A key advantage of style analysis over a constant-weight factor regression is that the factor benchmark is built from actual tradeable funds.
cards.explanation: Fama-French factors such as SMB and HML are not tradeable, so an alpha measured against them is not an implementable alternative. Style analysis builds the benchmark from real index funds and ETFs that an investor could have held.
cards.originalText: The factor benchmark is built from actual tradeable funds.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: A factor benchmark built with style analysis naturally overcomes the beta anomaly.
cards.explanation: Style analysis measures a fund's exposures. The beta anomaly is an empirical puzzle about the relationship between risk and return, and it survives any change in benchmark construction technique.
cards.originalText: The factor benchmark naturally overcomes the beta anomaly.
cards.correction: A factor benchmark built with style analysis does not overcome the beta anomaly.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: A factor benchmark built with style analysis does not overcome the beta anomaly.
cards.explanation: Style analysis measures a fund's exposures. The beta anomaly is an empirical puzzle about the relationship between risk and return, and it survives any change in benchmark construction technique.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: Statistical inference becomes easier once the factor loadings are allowed to vary over time.
cards.explanation: Time-varying loadings make inference harder: standard errors for alpha are difficult to compute when the factor loadings themselves vary. This is a technical cost of style analysis.
cards.correction: Statistical inference becomes harder once the factor loadings are allowed to vary over time.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: Statistical inference becomes harder once the factor loadings are allowed to vary over time.
cards.explanation: Time-varying loadings make inference harder: standard errors for alpha are difficult to compute when the factor loadings themselves vary. This is a technical cost of style analysis.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: In Sharpe's style analysis, fund returns are regressed on tradeable style index returns, with coefficients constrained to be non-negative and to sum to 100%, and the resulting weights describe a passive portfolio that would have matched the fund's risk exposures.
cards.explanation: The fund's return is the dependent variable and tradeable style indices are the regressors. Non-negativity and sum-to-one constraints make the fitted weights a feasible long-only allocation that replicates the fund's style.
cards.originalText: Fund returns are regressed on tradeable style index returns, with coefficients constrained to be non-negative and to sum to 100%, and the resulting weights describe a passive portfolio that would have matched the fund's risk exposures.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: In Sharpe's style analysis, fund returns are regressed on tradeable style index returns with no constraints, and the resulting weights describe the fund's active bets relative to its benchmark.
cards.explanation: Style analysis constrains coefficients to be non-negative and to sum to 100%, so the weights form a feasible allocation. The weights describe the fund's style; active bets are what remain after the style portfolio is subtracted.
cards.originalText: Fund returns are regressed on tradeable style index returns with no constraints, and the resulting weights describe the fund's active bets relative to its benchmark.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: In Sharpe's style analysis, style index returns are regressed on fund returns, with coefficients constrained to sum to 100%, and the intercept measures the fund's alpha.
cards.explanation: The regression runs the other way: fund returns are the dependent variable and style index returns are the regressors, with coefficients constrained to be non-negative and to sum to 100%.
cards.originalText: Style index returns are regressed on fund returns, with coefficients constrained to sum to 100%, and the intercept measures the fund's alpha.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to use style analysis to handle time-varying factor exposures
cards.reading: Reading 85: Ang, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)
cards.statement: In Sharpe's style analysis, fund returns are regressed on a single style index chosen to maximise the adjusted R-squared, and the slope coefficient measures the fund's style exposure.
cards.explanation: Style analysis regresses fund returns on a combination of several tradeable style indices, with non-negative weights summing to 100%. A fund's exposure is a mix of styles whose weights can move over time.
cards.originalText: Fund returns are regressed on a single style index chosen to maximise the adjusted R-squared, and the slope coefficient measures the fund's style exposure.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures and identify the circumstances under which each is most relevant
cards.statement: The information ratio incorporates the investor's risk aversion.
cards.explanation: The information ratio is a plain ratio of alpha to residual (tracking) risk and contains no risk-aversion parameter. Morningstar's risk-adjusted rating is the measure that uses a risk-aversion exponent.
cards.originalText: The information ratio, because it incorporates the investor's risk aversion.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures and identify the circumstances under which each is most relevant
cards.statement: The Sharpe ratio is the most robust performance measure for handling a mid-period change in a portfolio's risk.
cards.explanation: The Sharpe ratio estimates one standard deviation over the whole window, so a mid-period shift in risk produces a figure that describes neither regime. Morningstar's risk-adjusted rating is designed to handle changing risk.
cards.originalText: The Sharpe ratio, because it is the most robust measure for handling a mid-period change in risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures and identify the circumstances under which each is most relevant
cards.statement: Morningstar's risk-adjusted rating is designed to handle a mid-cycle change in a portfolio's risk.
cards.explanation: MRAR is built from period-by-period relative wealth with a risk-aversion exponent, so it accommodates and penalises risk that changes within the window. Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen's alpha and the information ratio all assume a stable risk level.
cards.originalText: Morningstar's risk-adjusted rating, because it is designed to handle a mid-cycle change in the portfolio's risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor's measure in comparing two portfolios, and the graphical representation of these measures
cards.statement: M-squared is the vertical distance between the market portfolio and the point on a managed portfolio P's capital allocation line whose standard deviation equals the market's; T-squared derives from the vertical distance between P and the security market line at P's beta.
cards.explanation: Both measures equalise risk first and then read a return difference on the vertical axis. M-squared slides along P's capital allocation line to the market's standard deviation; the vertical gap from P to the SML at P's beta is Jensen's alpha, from which T-squared is derived.
cards.originalText: M-squared is the vertical distance between the market portfolio and the point on P's capital allocation line whose standard deviation equals the market's; T-squared derives from the vertical distance between P and the security market line at P's beta.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor's measure in comparing two portfolios, and the graphical representation of these measures
cards.statement: M-squared is the horizontal distance between a managed portfolio P and the capital market line; T-squared is the horizontal distance between P and the security market line.
cards.explanation: Both M-squared and T-squared are differences in return, which is the vertical axis on both the CML and SML diagrams. A horizontal distance would be a difference in risk.
cards.originalText: M-squared is the horizontal distance between P and the capital market line; T-squared is the horizontal distance between P and the security market line.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor's measure in comparing two portfolios, and the graphical representation of these measures
cards.statement: M-squared is the difference in slope between a managed portfolio P's capital allocation line and the capital market line; T-squared is the difference in slope between the line joining the risk-free rate to P and the security market line.
cards.explanation: The slope difference between P's CAL and the CML is the difference in Sharpe ratios. M-squared is that difference multiplied by the market's standard deviation, which turns it into a return gap measured at equal total risk.
cards.originalText: M-squared is the difference in slope between P's capital allocation line and the capital market line; T-squared is the difference in slope between the line joining the risk-free rate to P and the security market line.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor's measure in comparing two portfolios, and the graphical representation of these measures
cards.statement: M-squared always agrees with the Treynor measure, and Jensen's alpha always agrees with the Sharpe ratio, but the two pairs can disagree when a manager's beta is far from 1.00.
cards.explanation: M-squared is a total-risk measure and is a strictly increasing transformation of the Sharpe ratio, so those two always rank alike. Jensen's alpha and Treynor both charge only for systematic risk. The total-risk and systematic-risk measures diverge when a portfolio carries a large amount of unsystematic risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor's measure in comparing two portfolios, and the graphical representation of these measures
cards.statement: The Sharpe ratio, M-squared, Jensen's alpha and the Treynor measure produce identical rankings, because each is a monotonic transformation of the portfolio's excess return.
cards.explanation: Sharpe and M-squared use total risk, while Jensen's alpha and Treynor use systematic risk. Because they use different risk definitions, the two groups can rank portfolios differently, especially when unsystematic risk is large.
cards.originalText: All four measures produce identical rankings, because each is a monotonic transformation of the portfolio's excess return.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor's measure in comparing two portfolios, and the graphical representation of these measures
cards.statement: The Sharpe ratio, M-squared, Jensen's alpha and the Treynor measure can each disagree with any of the others, because no two of them share a denominator.
cards.explanation: M-squared equals the market's standard deviation times the difference in Sharpe ratios, so it is a strictly increasing transformation of the Sharpe ratio and always ranks portfolios identically to it.
cards.originalText: The four measures can each disagree with any of the others, because no two of them share a denominator.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: A comparison universe median is not an investable strategy, whereas style analysis produces a benchmark built from index funds that a passive investor could actually have held.
cards.explanation: Performance evaluation asks whether a manager beat what a passive investor could have done. The median fund of a peer universe cannot be bought, but a style benchmark of index funds can, which is why style analysis gives a more meaningful comparison.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: A comparison universe requires a long history, whereas style analysis can be estimated from a single period of data.
cards.explanation: Style analysis is a regression and needs a reasonable run of periodic returns, and more still if the loadings are re-estimated each period.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: A comparison universe adjusts for risk, whereas style analysis measures raw return and is therefore simpler to explain to trustees.
cards.explanation: A comparison universe does not adjust for risk, which is one of its defects. Style analysis is a risk-exposure matching exercise that fits each manager's own exposures before judging performance.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: A comparison universe cannot detect survivorship bias, whereas style analysis eliminates it entirely.
cards.explanation: Survivorship bias arises from how the sample of funds is assembled, not from the choice of evaluation method. Style analysis does not eliminate it; the remedy is to include failed funds in the database.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: When a manager's return is decomposed using a style benchmark, style contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return, and active contribution is the manager's return less the style benchmark return.
cards.explanation: Each component is measured against its adjacent term: style against the market, and selection against the style benchmark. The style benchmark cancels, so the two components add up to the manager's total excess return over the market.
cards.originalText: Style contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return; active contribution is the manager's return less the style benchmark return.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: When a manager's return is decomposed using a style benchmark, style contribution is the manager's return less the style benchmark return, and active contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return.
cards.explanation: The labels are reversed. Style contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return; active (selection) contribution is the manager's return less the style benchmark return.
cards.originalText: Style contribution is the manager's return less the style benchmark return; active contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe style analysis
cards.statement: When a manager's return is decomposed using a style benchmark, style contribution is the manager's return less the market return, and active contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return.
cards.explanation: The manager's return less the market return is the total excess return, not the style component. Style contribution is the style benchmark less the market, and active contribution is the manager less the style benchmark.
cards.originalText: Style contribution is the manager's return less the market return; active contribution is the style benchmark return less the market return.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Alpha and the benchmark are simultaneously determined, so a sufficiently flexible search over factor sets will always be able to drive measured alpha toward zero.
cards.explanation: Alpha is defined only relative to a chosen factor set, so changing the set changes alpha. A search over many factor sets can manufacture almost any alpha, which is why a zero alpha found this way says nothing about skill.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: It is typically impossible to find an ex-post benchmark portfolio that produces no alpha.
cards.explanation: It is typically easy to find an ex-post benchmark portfolio that produces zero alpha. That is precisely why an alpha of zero found by searching over benchmarks is uninformative about skill.
cards.originalText: It is typically impossible to find an ex-post benchmark portfolio that produces no alpha, so John's result must be a computational error.
cards.correction: It is typically easy to find an ex-post benchmark portfolio that produces no alpha.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: It is typically easy to find an ex-post benchmark portfolio that produces no alpha.
cards.explanation: It is typically easy to find an ex-post benchmark portfolio that produces zero alpha. That is precisely why an alpha of zero found by searching over benchmarks is uninformative about skill.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Grossman and Stiglitz demonstrated that markets are perfectly efficient, so alpha does not exist.
cards.explanation: Grossman and Stiglitz argued the opposite: markets cannot be perfectly efficient, because if prices reflected all information nobody would pay to gather it. Some alpha must exist to reward information gathering.
cards.originalText: Grossman and Stiglitz demonstrated that markets are perfectly efficient, so alpha does not exist and the regressions are uninformative.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: It is impossible to evaluate strategies with nonlinear payoffs.
cards.explanation: Nonlinear strategies can be evaluated, for example by adding nonlinear terms such as max(R, 0) to the regression or by examining the full return distribution. The problem is only that a plain linear regression is the wrong tool.
cards.correction: It is possible to evaluate strategies with nonlinear payoffs.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: It is possible to evaluate strategies with nonlinear payoffs.
cards.explanation: Nonlinear strategies can be evaluated, for example by adding nonlinear terms such as max(R, 0) to the regression or by examining the full return distribution. The problem is only that a plain linear regression is the wrong tool.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Alpha is the residual term of the regression, not its intercept.
cards.explanation: Alpha is the regression intercept. The residual is the unexplained period-by-period error, and its standard deviation is the tracking error.
cards.correction: Alpha is the intercept of the regression, not its residual term.

changes.from: the residual term of the regression, not its intercept
changes.to: the intercept of the regression, not its residual term

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Alpha is the intercept of the regression, not its residual term.
cards.explanation: Alpha is the regression intercept. The residual is the unexplained period-by-period error, and its standard deviation is the tracking error.

changes.from: the residual term of the regression, not its intercept
changes.to: the intercept of the regression, not its residual term

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: A put-selling strategy's payoff is nonlinear and its return distribution is strongly negatively skewed, so a linear regression will report an alpha that reflects sold tail risk rather than skill.
cards.explanation: A short put collects small steady premiums in calm markets and suffers large losses in crashes. A linear regression over a sample without a severe drawdown fits a positive intercept that is really compensation for tail risk that has not yet materialised.
cards.originalText: The strategy's payoff is nonlinear and its return distribution is strongly negatively skewed, so a linear regression will report an alpha that reflects sold tail risk rather than skill.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Holding the confidence level and residual volatility fixed, the number of observations needed to establish that an alpha is statistically significant is inversely proportional to the alpha itself, so halving the alpha doubles the number of observations required.
cards.explanation: The t-statistic on alpha is alpha times the square root of N divided by residual volatility. Solving for N squares everything, so N is inversely proportional to the square of alpha: halving alpha quadruples the observations required.
cards.originalText: It falls in proportion to the alpha, so halving the alpha doubles the number of observations required.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Holding the confidence level and residual volatility fixed, the number of observations needed to establish that an alpha is statistically significant is inversely proportional to the square of the alpha, so halving the alpha quadruples the number of observations required.
cards.explanation: The t-statistic on alpha is alpha times the square root of N divided by residual volatility. Setting it equal to the critical value and solving gives N proportional to one over alpha squared, which is why detecting ordinary skill can take decades.
cards.originalText: It falls in proportion to the square of the alpha, so halving the alpha quadruples the number of observations required.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the difficulties in measuring the performance of actively managed portfolios
cards.statement: Holding the confidence level and residual volatility fixed, the number of observations needed to establish that an alpha is statistically significant does not depend on the size of the alpha.
cards.explanation: The required sample is inversely proportional to the square of alpha. A manager with a large alpha can be distinguished from luck far faster than one with a small alpha.
cards.originalText: It does not depend on the size of the alpha, only on the residual volatility and the confidence level.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Risk budgeting is a bottom-up process in which each portfolio manager sets an individual loss limit, with the plan's total risk emerging as the sum of those limits.
cards.explanation: Risk budgeting is top-down: a total risk appetite is set first and then allocated across activities. Because risk is not additive, summing individual limits gives the undiversified figure, which overstates total risk.
cards.originalText: A bottom-up process in which each portfolio manager sets an individual loss limit, with the plan's total risk emerging as the sum of those limits.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Risk budgeting is a top-down process of choosing and managing exposures to risk, in which a total risk appetite is set first and then allocated across activities.
cards.explanation: The board first fixes an overall risk appetite, typically as a total volatility or VaR, and that total is then allocated downward across asset classes and within each asset class across managers.
cards.originalText: A top-down process of choosing and managing exposures to risk, in which a total risk appetite is set first and then allocated across activities.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Risk budgeting is a regulatory capital allocation exercise in which risk-weighted assets are distributed across business lines to satisfy a minimum solvency ratio.
cards.explanation: That describes regulatory capital allocation under a banking solvency framework. Risk budgeting is an investment-management process driven by the organisation's own risk appetite.
cards.originalText: A regulatory capital allocation exercise in which risk-weighted assets are distributed across business lines to satisfy a minimum solvency ratio.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Risk budgeting is a performance measurement exercise in which realised losses are attributed to the managers responsible for them at the end of each period.
cards.explanation: That describes ex-post attribution. Risk budgeting is forward looking: it allocates a risk allowance before the risk is taken, which is what makes it a budget.
cards.originalText: A performance measurement exercise in which realised losses are attributed to the managers responsible for them at the end of each period.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: For each allocation of risk budget there should be a corresponding and acceptable return expectation, together with some sense of the expected variability around that expectation.
cards.explanation: Each risk allocation must carry a return expectation and a view on its variability, so that the aggregate of all allocations is consistent with the organisation's strategic objectives.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: The risk budget is the numeric blueprint that quantifies the vision set out in the risk plan, and it is often referred to as asset allocation.
cards.explanation: The risk plan sets the vision and points of success and failure; the risk budget is the numeric blueprint that gives it shape and form, and is often called asset allocation.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: An organisation puts its targets at risk only when it consumes more risk capital than budgeted, since consuming less than budgeted is always prudent.
cards.explanation: Targets are put at risk whenever risk capital is used in amounts inconsistent with policy, in either direction. Taking too little risk relative to budget causes returns to fall short of what the plan requires.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Define risk budgeting
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Risk monitoring should confirm not only that overall forecast tracking error matches the target but also that risk capital is being spent in the expected themes.
cards.explanation: Monitoring must check both the overall level of risk and its decomposition. A manager hitting the tracking error target while placing risk in the wrong themes is exhibiting style drift.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Absolute risk is the risk of a dollar loss owing to the policy mix selected by the fund; relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss over the horizon and may also be called asset risk.
cards.explanation: Absolute risk (also called asset risk) is the risk of a dollar loss over the horizon. Relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss relative to the benchmark. Loss owing to the chosen policy mix is policy-mix risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Absolute risk is the risk of a dollar loss over the horizon and is sometimes called asset risk; relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss in the fund relative to its benchmark.
cards.explanation: Absolute risk is the usual trading definition of loss over the horizon, also called asset risk. Relative risk is measured as the dollar difference between the fund return and a like amount invested in the benchmark.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Absolute risk is the risk of a dollar loss in the fund relative to its benchmark; relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss owing to the policy mix selected by the fund.
cards.explanation: Absolute risk is the risk of a dollar loss over the horizon. Relative risk is loss relative to the benchmark, and loss owing to the selected policy mix is policy-mix risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Absolute risk is the risk that assets will be insufficient to cover the fund's liabilities; relative risk is the summation of profits and losses across all active managers relative to their benchmarks.
cards.explanation: Those are the definitions of funding risk and active-management risk. Absolute risk is the risk of a dollar loss over the horizon, and relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss relative to the benchmark.
cards.correction: Funding risk is the risk that assets will be insufficient to cover the fund's liabilities; active-management risk is the summation of profits and losses across all active managers relative to their benchmarks.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Funding risk is the risk that assets will be insufficient to cover the fund's liabilities; active-management risk is the summation of profits and losses across all active managers relative to their benchmarks.
cards.explanation: Those are the definitions of funding risk and active-management risk. Absolute risk is the risk of a dollar loss over the horizon, and relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss relative to the benchmark.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Policy-mix risk represents the risk of a passive strategy, because the policy mix can generally be implemented by investing in passive funds.
cards.explanation: The policy-mix return is what the plan would earn by holding each sleeve's benchmark at policy weights, which is a passive strategy. Policy-mix risk is normally the dominant component of total risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Total fund VaR is obtained by adding the policy-mix VaR and the active-management VaR, since the two components are by construction uncorrelated.
cards.explanation: Total VaR depends on the policy-mix VaR, the active-management VaR and a cross-product term. The two components are not assumed to be uncorrelated, so their VaRs do not simply add.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Active-management risk is generally the larger of the two components, because manager deviations compound across a large pool of managers.
cards.explanation: Active-management risk is typically much smaller than policy-mix risk, because deviations of different managers from their benchmarks tend to diversify rather than compound.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: If all of a plan's managers make the same style shift at the same time, active-management risk falls, because their deviations become easier to forecast.
cards.explanation: A common style shift makes managers' deviations from their benchmarks co-move, so they no longer diversify away. This increases active-management risk.
cards.originalText: If all the plan's managers make the same style shift at the same time, active-management risk falls, because their deviations become easier to forecast.
cards.correction: If all of a plan's managers make the same style shift at the same time, active-management risk rises, because their deviations co-move.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: If all of a plan's managers make the same style shift at the same time, active-management risk rises, because their deviations co-move.
cards.explanation: A common style shift makes managers' deviations from their benchmarks co-move, so they no longer diversify away. This increases active-management risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: A plan sponsor that can absorb greater variations in funding costs can adopt a more volatile risk profile.
cards.explanation: Cash-flow risk is the risk of year-to-year fluctuations in contributions to the pension fund. It constrains sponsors differently: those with capacity to absorb funding variation can take more risk, so it does not uniformly prevent a more volatile profile.
cards.originalText: No, because a plan sponsor that can absorb greater variations in funding costs can adopt a more volatile risk profile.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Cash-flow risk is a component of funding risk rather than of sponsor risk, so it constrains the fund rather than the sponsor.
cards.explanation: Cash-flow risk is one of the two components of sponsor risk, alongside economic risk. Funding risk concerns whether assets cover liabilities; cash-flow risk concerns the volatility of the contributions the sponsor must make.
cards.originalText: No, because cash-flow risk is a component of funding risk rather than of sponsor risk, so it constrains the fund rather than the sponsor.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss owing to the total deviations of a plan's managers from the policy mix.
cards.explanation: That is the definition of active-management risk. Relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss in the fund relative to its benchmark.
cards.originalText: Relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss owing to the total deviations of the plan's managers from the policy mix.
cards.correction: Active-management risk is the risk of a dollar loss owing to the total deviations of a plan's managers from the policy mix.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Active-management risk is the risk of a dollar loss owing to the total deviations of a plan's managers from the policy mix.
cards.explanation: That is the definition of active-management risk. Relative risk is the risk of a dollar loss in the fund relative to its benchmark.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Policy-mix risk represents the risk of an active strategy, because the board actively selects the weights that define the mix.
cards.explanation: Policy-mix risk is the risk of a passive strategy, because the policy mix can generally be implemented by investing in passive funds.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Funding risk concerns whether the fund's assets will suffice to cover its liabilities, whereas sponsor risk concerns the effect of the fund on the economic value of the entity that stands behind it.
cards.explanation: Funding risk sits at the fund level and compares assets with liabilities. Sponsor risk extends surplus risk to the owner of the fund, through cash-flow risk and economic risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Economic risk is the risk of year-to-year fluctuations in the contributions a sponsor must make to the fund.
cards.explanation: That is the definition of cash-flow risk. Economic risk is the risk of variation in the total economic earnings of the plan sponsor; both are components of sponsor risk.
cards.correction: Cash-flow risk is the risk of year-to-year fluctuations in the contributions a sponsor must make to the fund.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Cash-flow risk is the risk of year-to-year fluctuations in the contributions a sponsor must make to the fund.
cards.explanation: That is the definition of cash-flow risk. Economic risk is the risk of variation in the total economic earnings of the plan sponsor; both are components of sponsor risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the use of VaR to monitor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: Using VaR to monitor risk in a large firm with many types of managers can help catch rogue traders and can detect changes in risk arising from changes in benchmark characteristics.
cards.explanation: Centralised VaR reporting reveals unauthorised positions that push risk outside the expected range. Because relative VaR is computed on the excess return over the benchmark, it also moves when the benchmark changes even if the portfolio does not.
cards.originalText: it can help catch rogue traders, and it can detect changes in risk arising from changes in benchmark characteristics.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the use of VaR to monitor risk
cards.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
cards.statement: VaR is not useful for monitoring risk in large firms, since aggregation across heterogeneous managers destroys the information content of the measure.
cards.explanation: Aggregation across heterogeneous managers is the reason a centralised risk measure such as VaR is needed. Firm-wide VaR helps catch rogue traders and detect shifts in risk from benchmark changes.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The primary risk of a dedicated short strategy is that rising share prices can trigger margin calls and forced covering of positions.
cards.explanation: A short position loses as the price rises, with no ceiling on the loss. Mounting losses trigger margin calls, and forced covering into a rising market (a short squeeze) compounds them. Markets also tend to drift upward, adding a structural headwind.
cards.originalText: Rising share prices can trigger margin calls and forced covering of positions.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Nonhedged equity retains full market exposure and relies on fundamental analysis, and may use leverage or derivatives to amplify even small mispricings.
cards.explanation: Nonhedged equity is long only, so it keeps full market exposure. It relies on concentrated fundamental stock picking and often uses leverage or derivatives to magnify small mispricings.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Equity long/short eliminates all factor exposures, since the offsetting long and short positions are constructed to neutralise every systematic risk.
cards.explanation: Equity long/short aims to reduce market risk, and managers use factor models to mitigate remaining factor exposures beyond beta. Residual factor exposures remain; eliminating all of them is not achievable.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Nonhedged equity differs from a traditional mutual fund principally in that it diversifies more broadly across names to control risk.
cards.explanation: Broad diversification is the mutual fund's approach to risk. Nonhedged equity hedge funds are distinguished by concentration and the use of leverage.
cards.correction: A traditional mutual fund differs from nonhedged equity principally in that it diversifies more broadly across names to control risk.

changes.from: Nonhedged equity differs from a traditional mutual fund
changes.to: A traditional mutual fund differs from nonhedged equity

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
