cards.statement: A traditional mutual fund differs from nonhedged equity principally in that it diversifies more broadly across names to control risk.
cards.explanation: Broad diversification is the mutual fund's approach to risk. Nonhedged equity hedge funds are distinguished by concentration and the use of leverage.

changes.from: Nonhedged equity differs from a traditional mutual fund
changes.to: A traditional mutual fund differs from nonhedged equity

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Dedicated short strategies and equity long/short strategies share the same primary risk, namely that the manager's fundamental analysis of the long book proves incorrect.
cards.explanation: A dedicated short strategy has no long book. Its primary risk is rising prices on its short positions, leading to margin calls and forced covering.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Global macro managers take large, often leveraged, directional positions across equities, fixed income, interest rates, currencies and commodities, frequently expressed through derivatives.
cards.explanation: Global macro makes large, leveraged bets on anticipated price movements across broad markets, often using derivatives linked to a wide range of underlying asset classes and indices.
cards.originalText: Managers take large, often leveraged, directional positions across equities, fixed income, interest rates, currencies and commodities, frequently expressed through derivatives.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Unlike mutual funds, which are restricted to their mandated investment areas, global macro funds have broad discretion in selecting opportunities across global markets.
cards.explanation: Global macro managers can allocate capital across sectors, regions and asset classes as they anticipate changes in international macroeconomic trends, unlike mutual funds bound to a mandate.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Global macro funds tend to concentrate in less liquid instruments, because the illiquidity premium is the principal source of their return.
cards.explanation: Global macro funds tend to trade more liquid instruments, since expressing large directional views requires deep markets that can absorb and exit big positions. Their returns come from macroeconomic views, not an illiquidity premium.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Global macro managers consider economic forecasts, international capital flows, interest rate trends, political developments and economic policies when forming positions.
cards.explanation: Global macro positions are driven by top-down views on international macroeconomic trends, which draw on forecasts, capital flows, rates, politics and policy.
cards.originalText: Managers consider economic forecasts, international capital flows, interest rate trends, political developments and economic policies when forming positions.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Shorting the on-the-run 30-year Treasury while buying the cheaper off-the-run 29.5-year issue is relative value arbitrage.
cards.explanation: That trade is the textbook example of fixed-income arbitrage, which profits as the on-the-run liquidity premium fades. Relative value arbitrage is typified by pairs trading in related stocks.
cards.correction: Shorting the on-the-run 30-year Treasury while buying the cheaper off-the-run 29.5-year issue is fixed-income arbitrage.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Shorting the on-the-run 30-year Treasury while buying the cheaper off-the-run 29.5-year issue is fixed-income arbitrage.
cards.explanation: That trade is the textbook example of fixed-income arbitrage, which profits as the on-the-run liquidity premium fades. Relative value arbitrage is typified by pairs trading in related stocks.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Buying one stock and shorting a peer whose price relationship has temporarily diverged without fundamental news is relative value arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Pairs trading is the long-established relative value arbitrage strategy. The absence of fundamental news is what makes the divergence a mispricing expected to converge rather than new information.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Buying a target company's stock and shorting the acquirer's stock in a share-for-share deal is convertible arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Long target, short acquirer in a stock-for-stock deal is merger arbitrage, an event-driven strategy. Convertible arbitrage buys a convertible bond and shorts the underlying stock.
cards.correction: Buying a target company's stock and shorting the acquirer's stock in a share-for-share deal is merger arbitrage.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Buying a target company's stock and shorting the acquirer's stock in a share-for-share deal is merger arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Long target, short acquirer in a stock-for-stock deal is merger arbitrage, an event-driven strategy. Convertible arbitrage buys a convertible bond and shorts the underlying stock.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to neutralise equity exposure is fixed-income arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock is convertible arbitrage. Fixed-income arbitrage exploits mispricings between related interest-rate instruments, such as on-the-run versus off-the-run Treasuries.
cards.correction: Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to neutralise equity exposure is convertible arbitrage.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to neutralise equity exposure is convertible arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock is convertible arbitrage. Fixed-income arbitrage exploits mispricings between related interest-rate instruments, such as on-the-run versus off-the-run Treasuries.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The defining characteristic of a convertible arbitrage strategy is buying undervalued sovereign bonds and shorting corporate bonds.
cards.explanation: That is a credit or sovereign spread trade within fixed-income arbitrage. Convertible arbitrage buys a convertible bond and shorts the underlying stock to hedge its equity exposure.
cards.originalText: Buying undervalued sovereign bonds and shorting corporate bonds.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The defining characteristic of a convertible arbitrage strategy is taking offsetting long and short positions across different yield curves.
cards.explanation: Offsetting positions across yield curves is a cross-market fixed-income arbitrage trade. Convertible arbitrage buys a convertible bond and shorts the underlying stock.
cards.originalText: Taking offsetting long and short positions across different yield curves.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The defining characteristic of a convertible arbitrage strategy is buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to hedge equity exposure.
cards.explanation: A convertible bond contains an embedded equity call. The arbitrageur buys the convertible and shorts the underlying shares in the delta-implied amount to hedge the share-price sensitivity, keeping exposure to coupons, rates and credit.
cards.originalText: Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to hedge equity exposure.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The defining characteristic of a convertible arbitrage strategy is buying stocks with high dividend yields while shorting stocks with relatively low dividend yields.
cards.explanation: That is a dividend-yield factor trade. In convertible arbitrage, dividends appear only as a cost owed to the lender of the shorted shares; the strategy itself is long a convertible bond and short the underlying stock.
cards.originalText: Buying stocks with high dividend yields while shorting stocks with relatively low dividend yields.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Because the relationship between the stock price and the convertible bond price is nonlinear, a move in the stock in either direction tends to produce a gain on a delta-hedged convertible arbitrage position, since the gain on one leg exceeds the loss on the other.
cards.explanation: The short stock hedge is linear in the share price but the convertible is convex. When the stock rises the bond gains at an accelerating rate, and when it falls the bond loses at a decelerating rate, so the hedged position gains on moves of either sign. This is called monetising volatility.
cards.originalText: Because the relationship between the stock price and the convertible bond price is nonlinear, a move in the stock in either direction tends to produce a gain on the hedged position, since the gain on one leg exceeds the loss on the other.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Excess leverage, which magnifies losses as readily as it magnifies gains, is one of the standard reasons hedge funds have failed.
cards.explanation: Excess leverage is on the standard list of reasons for hedge fund failure, closely related to poor investment decisions. Leverage cuts both ways, magnifying losses just as it magnifies gains.
cards.originalText: Excess leverage, which magnifies losses as readily as it magnifies gains

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Lack of liquidity, where simultaneous withdrawals create a cash-flow squeeze the fund cannot meet, is one of the standard reasons hedge funds have failed.
cards.explanation: Lack of liquidity is on the standard list of reasons for hedge fund failure: too many withdrawals and redemptions at once can create a cash-flow crisis the fund cannot meet.
cards.originalText: Lack of liquidity, where simultaneous withdrawals create a cash-flow squeeze the fund cannot meet

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Excessive concentration of the manager's personal wealth in the fund, which distorts the manager's incentives toward risk aversion, is one of the standard reasons hedge funds have failed.
cards.explanation: This is not a recognised reason for failure. Manager co-investment is a recommended way to align the manager's interests with investors'. The standard reasons include poor investment decisions, fraud, extreme events, excess leverage, lack of liquidity, poor controls, insufficient questioning and insufficient attention to returns.
cards.originalText: Excessive concentration of the manager's personal wealth in the fund, which distorts the manager's incentives toward risk aversion

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Poor controls, where a lack of supervision permits risk taking large enough to bankrupt the fund, is one of the standard reasons hedge funds have failed.
cards.explanation: Poor controls is on the standard list of reasons for hedge fund failure and is closely related to fraud: without adequate supervision, traders can take risks large enough to bring down the fund.
cards.originalText: Poor controls, where a lack of supervision permits risk taking large enough to bankrupt the fund

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy involved selling an out-of-the-money call option.
cards.explanation: The strategy had three steps: hold stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100, write out-of-the-money index calls to create a ceiling, and buy out-of-the-money index puts to create a floor.
cards.originalText: Part of the strategy involved selling an out-of-the-money call option.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: In Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy, a floor value was created by purchasing an out-of-the-money put option.
cards.explanation: The long out-of-the-money put on the S&P 100 created the floor, while the short out-of-the-money call created a ceiling. Together they form a collar around the equity portfolio.
cards.originalText: A floor value was created by purchasing an out-of-the-money put option.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy required a long position in a portfolio of stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100.
cards.explanation: The equity portfolio had to track the S&P 100 closely so that S&P 100 index puts and calls would be an effective hedge. Calls were written and puts bought on that index.
cards.originalText: A long position in a portfolio of stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100 was required.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: In Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy, gains on the equity portfolio were supplemented by gains on a long out-of-the-money call option position.
cards.explanation: The call position was short, not long. Writing out-of-the-money calls created a ceiling: as stocks rose, portfolio gains were offset by the rising liability on the short calls.
cards.originalText: Gains on the equity portfolio were supplemented by gains on a long out-of-the-money call option position.
cards.correction: In Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy, gains on the equity portfolio were offset by losses on a short out-of-the-money call option position.

changes.from: supplemented by gains on a long
changes.to: offset by losses on a short

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: In Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy, gains on the equity portfolio were offset by losses on a short out-of-the-money call option position.
cards.explanation: The call position was short, not long. Writing out-of-the-money calls created a ceiling: as stocks rose, portfolio gains were offset by the rising liability on the short calls.

changes.from: supplemented by gains on a long
changes.to: offset by losses on a short

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds were significantly higher than the S&P 100, and more volatile.
cards.explanation: Madoff's reported returns were a steady 8% to 12% a year, roughly comparable to the S&P 100, with dramatically lower volatility and almost no down months.
cards.originalText: significantly higher than the S&P 100, and more volatile.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds were significantly higher than the S&P 100, and much less volatile.
cards.explanation: The reported returns were comparable to the S&P 100, not significantly higher. What was implausible was the extremely low volatility and the absence of any down year.
cards.originalText: significantly higher than the S&P 100, and much less volatile.
cards.correction: Returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds were approximately the same as the S&P 100, and much less volatile.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds were approximately the same as the S&P 100, and much less volatile.
cards.explanation: The reported returns were comparable to the S&P 100, not significantly higher. What was implausible was the extremely low volatility and the absence of any down year.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds were approximately the same as the S&P 100, but with much lower volatility.
cards.explanation: Madoff reported a steady 8% to 12% a year, comparable to the index, but with far lower volatility, more than 95% positive months and no down years. The implausibly smooth return stream was the key red flag.
cards.originalText: approximately the same as the S&P 100, but with much lower volatility.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds were significantly lower than the S&P 100, but as stable as short-term Treasury bills.
cards.explanation: Reported returns of 8% to 12% a year were roughly comparable to the S&P 100, not significantly lower. The anomaly was their unusually low volatility.
cards.originalText: significantly lower than the S&P 100, but as stable as short-term Treasury bills.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities began in 1960 as an investment advisory business and later added a brokerage arm, which was the source of its eventual collapse.
cards.explanation: The sequence is reversed. The firm began in 1960 as a brokerage business and later expanded into investment advisory, and it was the advisory business that turned out to be a Ponzi scheme.
cards.originalText: The firm began in 1960 as an investment advisory business and later added a brokerage arm, which was the source of its eventual collapse.
cards.correction: Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities began in 1960 as a brokerage business and later added an investment advisory arm, which was the source of its eventual collapse.

changes.from: an investment advisory business and later added a brokerage arm
changes.to: a brokerage business and later added an investment advisory arm

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities began in 1960 as a brokerage business and later added an investment advisory arm, which was the source of its eventual collapse.
cards.explanation: The sequence is reversed. The firm began in 1960 as a brokerage business and later expanded into investment advisory, and it was the advisory business that turned out to be a Ponzi scheme.

changes.from: an investment advisory business and later added a brokerage arm
changes.to: a brokerage business and later added an investment advisory arm

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities began in 1960 as a brokerage business quoting bid and ask prices and executing over-the-counter trades, later adopting electronic trading and eventually expanding into the investment advisory business that collapsed.
cards.explanation: The firm started as an over-the-counter brokerage, adopted electronic trading through the Cincinnati Stock Exchange, and later added the investment advisory business, which was the source of the fraud and collapse.
cards.originalText: The firm began in 1960 as a brokerage business quoting bid and ask prices and executing over-the-counter trades, later adopting electronic trading and eventually expanding into the investment advisory business that collapsed.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: The Madoff scheme was uncovered by an SEC examination in December 2008 following repeated warnings from a former portfolio manager.
cards.explanation: The scheme was not uncovered by an investigation. As markets fell in 2008, redemption requests could not be met, and on 10 December 2008 Madoff confessed to his family, who reported him; he was arrested the next day.
cards.originalText: The scheme was uncovered by an SEC examination in December 2008 following repeated warnings from a former portfolio manager.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Investors in Madoff's feeder funds were able to conduct direct due diligence on the firm itself, but chose not to exercise that right.
cards.explanation: Feeder-fund investors could not conduct direct due diligence on Madoff's firm. On-site due diligence was denied or heavily restricted, and Madoff refused to discuss his strategy.
cards.originalText: Investors in the feeder funds were able to conduct direct due diligence on the firm itself, but chose not to exercise that right.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: In the Madoff case, Form 13F filings showed holdings in small, non-S&P 100 companies, inconsistent with the claimed strategy focus.
cards.explanation: Madoff claimed a split-strike strategy built on S&P 100 stocks, but his 13F filings showed small non-S&P 100 holdings. This inconsistency between the stated strategy and disclosed activity was an investment red flag.
cards.originalText: Form 13F filings showed holdings in small, non-S&P 100 companies, inconsistent with the claimed strategy focus.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario (MDS) approach removes subjectivity entirely by relying on fully automated statistical models.
cards.explanation: The MDS approach explicitly retains an element of subjectivity, with expert judgement as its input. Its value lies in making that subjectivity transparent and open to challenge, not in removing it.
cards.originalText: removes subjectivity entirely by relying on fully automated statistical models.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario (MDS) approach relies solely on historical relationships between market variables to estimate profit and loss impacts.
cards.explanation: Sole reliance on historical relationships was the defect of pre-crisis stress testing, since those relationships broke down in 2007-2009. MDS builds forward-looking scenarios from aggregated expert views.
cards.originalText: relies solely on historical relationships between market variables to estimate profit and loss impacts.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario (MDS) approach eliminates the need for covariance matrices by focusing only on individual asset-level shocks.
cards.explanation: The covariance matrix is central to MDS. Shocks to policy variables are passed through a covariance matrix to imply the other shocks and to assess plausibility, and the choice of matrix materially affects the resulting z-scores.
cards.originalText: eliminates the need for covariance matrices by focusing only on individual asset-level shocks.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario (MDS) approach provides a structured framework for aggregating diverse expert opinions into forward-looking scenarios.
cards.explanation: MDS gathers input from investment professionals across asset classes, regions and areas of expertise, which risk management aggregates centrally. This addresses the reliance of pre-crisis stress tests on historical relationships that broke down.
cards.originalText: provides a structured framework for aggregating diverse expert opinions into forward-looking scenarios.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: Surowiecki's criteria for improving decisions by aggregating information from many individuals include that each individual should possess specialised knowledge that is not available to others.
cards.explanation: Surowiecki's three criteria are: specialised private knowledge, independence of opinion free of groupthink, and an objective mechanism for aggregating private views. MDS meets the first by drawing on a diverse group of professionals.
cards.originalText: Each individual should possess specialised knowledge that is not available to others.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: Surowiecki's criteria for improving decisions by aggregating information from many individuals include that individual opinions must be independent and not influenced by groupthink.
cards.explanation: Independence of opinion is one of Surowiecki's three criteria. In the MDS approach, views are collected privately before aggregation rather than formed together in a room.
cards.originalText: Individual opinions must be independent and not influenced by groupthink.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: Surowiecki's criteria for improving decisions by aggregating information from many individuals include that contributors must have comparable levels of seniority, so that no single view carries disproportionate weight.
cards.explanation: Comparable seniority is not one of the criteria. Surowiecki requires specialised knowledge, independent opinions, and an objective aggregation mechanism; diversity of expertise often implies differences in rank.
cards.originalText: The individuals contributing must have comparable levels of seniority, so that no single view carries disproportionate weight.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: Surowiecki's criteria for improving decisions by aggregating information from many individuals include that there must be an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.
cards.explanation: An objective aggregation mechanism is Surowiecki's third criterion. MDS satisfies it through a centralised risk-management process, supported by statistical tools such as the Mahalanobis distance.
cards.originalText: There must be an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario process, risk managers, investors and economists identify a current issue; idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum are defined; those outcomes are translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables; the shocks are assessed for plausibility and passed through a covariance matrix; the scenario is refined over several iterations; the finalised shocks are run through a valuation engine to produce a portfolio profit and loss.
cards.explanation: The MDS process starts from a view about the world rather than from the portfolio. Narrative outcomes become shocks on policy variables, plausibility is checked and other shocks are implied via the covariance matrix, and only after iterative refinement is the portfolio revalued.
cards.originalText: Risk managers, investors and economists identify a current issue; idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum are defined; those outcomes are translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables; the shocks are assessed for plausibility and passed through a covariance matrix; the scenario is refined over several iterations; the finalised shocks are run through a valuation engine to produce a portfolio profit and loss.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario process, the portfolio is first run through a valuation engine to identify its largest exposures; shocks are then designed to target those exposures specifically; the resulting scenario is accepted without further iteration, since it is by construction the worst case for that portfolio.
cards.explanation: MDS scenarios originate in views about current market issues, not in the portfolio's known exposures, and they are refined over several iterations. Valuation of the portfolio is the final step.
cards.originalText: The portfolio is first run through a valuation engine to identify its largest exposures; shocks are then designed to target those exposures specifically; the resulting scenario is accepted without further iteration, since it is by construction the worst case for that portfolio.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario process, historical crisis episodes are ranked by severity; the most severe is selected; its realised shocks are applied unchanged to the current portfolio; the resulting profit and loss becomes the stress result.
cards.explanation: That describes historical scenario replay. MDS is forward looking: experts define outcomes for current issues, translate them into policy-variable shocks and refine them. History enters only as a calibration reference through the risk ruler.
cards.originalText: Historical crisis episodes are ranked by severity; the most severe is selected; its realised shocks are applied unchanged to the current portfolio; the resulting profit and loss becomes the stress result.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario process, shocks are applied to every risk factor simultaneously and independently; a covariance matrix is then fitted to the resulting perturbation vector; the scenario is accepted if the fitted matrix matches the historical one.
cards.explanation: In MDS a small set of policy variables is shocked, and the covariance matrix is an input used to imply the non-policy shocks and assess plausibility. It is not fitted to the scenario after the fact.
cards.originalText: Shocks are applied to every risk factor simultaneously and independently; a covariance matrix is then fitted to the resulting perturbation vector; the scenario is accepted if the fitted matrix matches the historical one.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach is unsound, because any framework retaining an element of subjectivity cannot produce a defensible stress result.
cards.explanation: Every scenario framework retains judgement. Although MDS is partly subjective, it is highly valuable because it forces risk takers to quantify their views in a structured way so they can be challenged and refined.
cards.originalText: The approach is unsound, because any framework retaining an element of subjectivity cannot produce a defensible stress result.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach retains an element of subjectivity, and that is precisely where its value lies: it forces risk takers through a structured process that quantifies their subjective views, which can then be made transparent, challenged and refined.
cards.explanation: Subjectivity is a limitation of MDS but not a fatal one. Quantifying expert views makes them transparent, and the iterative feedback process of challenge and refinement is an essential part of effective portfolio risk management.
cards.originalText: The approach retains an element of subjectivity, and that is precisely where its value lies: it forces risk takers through a structured process that quantifies their subjective views, which can then be made transparent, challenged and refined.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach is sound because the Mahalanobis distance provides an objective test that accepts or rejects each proposed scenario, removing the need for iteration.
cards.explanation: The Mahalanobis distance assesses the plausibility and magnitude of a scenario; it does not give a binary accept-or-reject verdict. The MDS process explicitly proceeds through several iterations before a collective scenario is agreed.
cards.originalText: The approach is sound because the Mahalanobis distance provides an objective test that accepts or rejects each proposed scenario, removing the need for iteration.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach is sound but adds little beyond VaR, since both ultimately rely on the same covariance matrix and therefore produce the same tail estimates.
cards.explanation: MDS uses the covariance matrix to imply non-policy shocks and test plausibility, but the scenario itself is a forward-looking view rather than a distributional percentile. It targets events for which history is uninformative, which is where VaR failed in 2008.
cards.originalText: The approach is sound but adds little beyond VaR, since both ultimately rely on the same covariance matrix and therefore produce the same tail estimates.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: Of two scenarios, the one with the higher scenario z-score is considered more plausible, because a higher score indicates greater consistency with the historical covariance structure.
cards.explanation: A higher scenario z-score means a more severe and less plausible scenario. Of two scenarios, the one with the lower scenario z-score is considered more plausible.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: Of two scenarios, the one with the lower scenario z-score is considered more plausible, and a risk ruler arranges historical events by their z-scores to help assign a score to a hypothetical future event.
cards.explanation: The scenario z-score measures severity in standard deviations, so lower means more plausible. For hypothetical events, analysts compare against a risk ruler of past episodes ranked by z-score.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: The scenario z-score gives the absolute probability of a scenario directly, which is why it is preferred to the Mahalanobis distance.
cards.explanation: Scenario z-scores measure relative probability under an elliptical distribution assumption. Converting them into absolute probabilities requires further parametric or nonparametric assumptions.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: The scenario z-score is designed to make the Mahalanobis distance grow in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables, so that scenarios with more variables are penalised appropriately.
cards.explanation: The scenario z-score exists to prevent the Mahalanobis distance from growing in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables. Without that rescaling, richly specified scenarios would mechanically look implausible.
cards.correction: The scenario z-score is designed to stop the Mahalanobis distance growing in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables, so that scenarios with more variables are not penalised mechanically.

changes.from: designed to make the Mahalanobis distance grow
changes.to: designed to stop the Mahalanobis distance growing

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: The scenario z-score is designed to stop the Mahalanobis distance growing in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables, so that scenarios with more variables are not penalised mechanically.
cards.explanation: The scenario z-score exists to prevent the Mahalanobis distance from growing in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables. Without that rescaling, richly specified scenarios would mechanically look implausible.

changes.from: designed to make the Mahalanobis distance grow
changes.to: designed to stop the Mahalanobis distance growing

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: In Kinlaw and Turkington's decomposition of the scenario z-score, the magnitude component is isolated by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero.
cards.explanation: Setting all correlations to zero makes the covariance matrix diagonal and removes all cross-terms, so each shock is measured only against its own volatility. The result is the volatility z-score, which captures magnitude alone.
cards.originalText: By computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: In Kinlaw and Turkington's decomposition of the scenario z-score, the magnitude component is isolated by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are one.
cards.explanation: The magnitude component, the volatility z-score, assumes all correlations are zero, which removes the cross-terms. Perfect correlation is the most restrictive assumption, not a neutral one.
cards.originalText: By computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are one.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: In Kinlaw and Turkington's decomposition of the scenario z-score, the magnitude component is isolated by dividing the scenario z-score by the number of policy variables.
cards.explanation: The magnitude component, the volatility z-score, is obtained by setting all correlations to zero. Dividing by the number of variables would not remove the correlation information.
cards.originalText: By dividing the scenario z-score by the number of policy variables, which removes the dimensional effect of the shock vector.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: In Kinlaw and Turkington's decomposition of the scenario z-score, the magnitude component is isolated by computing the scenario z-score using only the largest individual factor shock.
cards.explanation: The magnitude of a multivariate scenario depends on all the shocks. The volatility z-score isolates magnitude by keeping every shock but setting all correlations to zero.
cards.originalText: By computing the scenario z-score using only the largest individual factor shock, since that shock dominates the magnitude of the scenario.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: When constructing a market-driven scenario for a severe equity market crash, the covariance matrix used to compute z-scores should be estimated from periods that experienced similar crashes, because correlations among risky assets typically spike during crises, and relying only on normal data would understate the severity of the stress.
cards.explanation: The choice of covariance matrix significantly affects the resulting z-scores. Because correlations among risky assets rise sharply in crises, a matrix calibrated on comparable crash periods captures crisis co-movement better than one built from normal-market data.
cards.originalText: Use a matrix estimated from periods that experienced similar crashes, because correlations among risky assets typically spike during crises, and relying only on normal data would understate the severity of the stress.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario approach, the choice of covariance matrix does not materially matter, because the scenario z-score is normalised for the covariance structure and is therefore invariant to the matrix selected.
cards.explanation: The choice of covariance matrix significantly affects the resulting z-scores and produces a different risk ruler for the same events. Scale invariance is a property of the correlation z-score with respect to shock size, not of any measure with respect to the matrix.
cards.originalText: The choice does not materially matter, because the scenario z-score is normalised for the covariance structure and is therefore invariant to the matrix selected.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Section 3(c)(1) applies where the fund has fewer than 100 investors; Section 3(c)(7) applies where the fund is limited to qualified purchasers, meaning individuals with more than USD 5 million in investment assets, but a fund relying on it must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 if it has 500 or more investors.
cards.explanation: These are the two Investment Company Act of 1940 exemptions hedge funds rely on to avoid mutual-fund-style registration. The qualified-purchaser exemption does not carry over to the 1934 Act, which is triggered at 500 or more investors.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Section 3(c)(1) applies where the fund has fewer than 500 investors; Section 3(c)(7) applies where the fund is limited to accredited investors, and carries no further registration trigger at any investor count.
cards.explanation: The first exemption requires fewer than 100 investors. The second requires the fund to be limited to qualified purchasers (individuals with more than USD 5 million in investment assets), and such a fund with 500 or more investors must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Section 3(c)(1) applies where the fund has fewer than 100 investors; Section 3(c)(7) applies where the fund is limited to qualified purchasers, and a fund relying on either exemption is permanently exempt from all federal securities registration.
cards.explanation: The two tests are right, but the exemptions apply only under the Investment Company Act of 1940. A qualified-purchaser fund with 500 or more investors must still register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Both Investment Company Act exemptions turn on assets under management rather than investor count, with Section 3(c)(1) applying below USD 150 million and Section 3(c)(7) below USD 1.5 billion.
cards.explanation: The two Investment Company Act exemptions turn on having fewer than 100 investors, or on limiting the fund to qualified purchasers. The USD 150 million and USD 1.5 billion figures are Form PF filing thresholds for registered advisers.
cards.originalText: Both exemptions turn on assets under management rather than investor count, with Section 3(c)(1) applying below USD 150 million and Section 3(c)(7) below USD 1.5 billion.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act, the Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act, eliminated the private adviser exemption, so the former 15-client threshold is no longer relevant and managers must register with the SEC; it also mandates reporting to the SEC and the Financial Stability Oversight Council and introduced Form PF, filed annually by advisers with at least USD 150 million in AUM and quarterly by those with more than USD 1.5 billion.
cards.explanation: After the 2006 court decision overturning the SEC's registration rule, Dodd-Frank Title IV brought hedge fund advisers under SEC registration. Form PF filing frequency scales with AUM: annual from USD 150 million and quarterly above USD 1.5 billion.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act preserved the private adviser exemption but raised its threshold from 15 to 100 funds, and introduced Form PF as a voluntary disclosure regime administered by the Alternative Investment Management Association.
cards.explanation: Title IV eliminated the private adviser exemption. Form PF is mandatory and filed with the SEC; AIMA's voluntary valuation guide is a separate self-regulatory initiative.
cards.originalText: Title IV preserved the private adviser exemption but raised its threshold from 15 to 100 funds, and introduced Form PF as a voluntary disclosure regime administered by the Alternative Investment Management Association.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: The SEC successfully mandated hedge fund registration through a 2004 rulemaking, which was upheld on appeal in 2006 and made Dodd-Frank's registration provisions redundant.
cards.explanation: The SEC's 2004 registration rule was overturned by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in 2006. Mandatory registration of hedge fund advisers came only with Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act eliminated the private adviser exemption, and Form PF is filed quarterly by all registered advisers regardless of assets under management, which is what makes the data comparable across the industry.
cards.explanation: Form PF has a two-tier structure: advisers with at least USD 150 million in AUM file annually, and those with more than USD 1.5 billion file quarterly.
cards.originalText: Title IV eliminated the private adviser exemption, and Form PF is filed quarterly by all registered advisers regardless of assets under management, which is what makes the data comparable across the industry.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: In hedge fund regulation, investor protection is addressed by restricting participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate hedge fund risks; market integrity by monitoring insider trading under the same rules applied across financial markets; and financial stability by limiting leverage and requiring timely and accurate posting of collateral.
cards.explanation: Each of the three regulatory objectives has its own mechanism. Accredited-investor and qualified-purchaser tests protect investors, general market rules police insider trading, and leverage limits and collateral requirements address systemic stability.
cards.originalText: Investor protection is addressed by restricting participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate hedge fund risks; market integrity by monitoring insider trading under the same rules applied across financial markets; and financial stability by limiting leverage and requiring timely and accurate posting of collateral.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: In hedge fund regulation, investor protection is addressed by limiting leverage; market integrity by restricting participation to sophisticated investors; and financial stability by monitoring insider trading.
cards.explanation: The mechanisms are rotated. Investor protection restricts participation to sophisticated investors, market integrity relies on insider-trading rules applied across markets, and financial stability relies on leverage limits and collateral posting.
cards.originalText: Investor protection is addressed by limiting leverage; market integrity by restricting participation to sophisticated investors; and financial stability by monitoring insider trading.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds
cards.statement: In hedge fund regulation, investor protection is addressed by mandatory public disclosure of positions; market integrity by capping performance fees; and financial stability by requiring hedge funds to hold regulatory capital on the same basis as banks.
cards.explanation: Hedge funds are not required to disclose positions publicly, performance-fee limits apply to registered mutual funds rather than hedge funds, and hedge funds hold no bank-style regulatory capital. The actual mechanisms are participation limits, insider-trading rules, and leverage and collateral requirements.
cards.originalText: Investor protection is addressed by mandatory public disclosure of positions; market integrity by capping performance fees; and financial stability by requiring hedge funds to hold regulatory capital on the same basis as banks.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: A hedge fund is typically organised as a limited partnership, in which the hedge fund manager serves as the general partner and the investors are the limited partners, usually as an open-ended partnership so the fund can issue new shares to incoming investors and redeem shares for those exiting, subject to any lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.
cards.explanation: The manager as general partner runs the fund; investors as limited partners contribute capital without managing it, which limits their liability. Hedge funds are open-ended, with redemptions controlled by lockups and gates.
cards.originalText: A limited partnership, in which the hedge fund manager serves as the general partner and the investors are the limited partners, usually organised as an open-ended partnership so the fund can issue new shares to incoming investors and redeem shares for those exiting, subject to any lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: A hedge fund is typically organised as a limited partnership, in which the investors serve as general partners so as to retain control over investment decisions, and the manager acts as a limited partner compensated through carried interest.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed. The manager is the general partner and the investors are limited partners; investors acting as general partners would take on management responsibility and unlimited liability.
cards.originalText: A limited partnership, in which the investors serve as general partners so as to retain control over investment decisions, and the manager acts as a limited partner compensated through carried interest.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: A hedge fund is typically organised as a closed-end corporation, which prevents redemptions entirely and is the reason lockups and gates are unnecessary in hedge fund documentation.
cards.explanation: Hedge funds are typically open-ended limited partnerships. Lockups and gates exist precisely because redemptions are permitted and need to be controlled.
cards.originalText: A closed-end corporation, which prevents redemptions entirely and is the reason lockups and gates are unnecessary in hedge fund documentation.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: A hedge fund is typically organised as a limited partnership structured as a closed-end vehicle, matching the private equity model, which is why hedge fund capital is committed rather than subscribed.
cards.explanation: The limited partnership form is right, but hedge funds are open-ended: capital is subscribed and redeemable, subject to lockups and gates. Committed, drawn-down capital is the closed-end private equity model.
cards.originalText: A limited partnership organised as a closed-end vehicle, matching the private equity model, which is why hedge fund capital is committed rather than subscribed.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: In a U.S.-domiciled hedge fund's master-feeder structure, all capital is pooled and all trading occurs in the master fund, which is funded by multiple feeder vehicles designed for different investor groups; typically one feeder serves onshore investors and another serves offshore investors, with the offshore feeder generally used for non-U.S. investors and for U.S. tax-exempt investors such as pension funds. The structure avoids multiple layers of taxation and allows tax-exempt investors to participate tax-efficiently.
cards.explanation: The master fund holds a single portfolio; feeders are organised by investor group. U.S. tax-exempt investors use the offshore feeder because investing through an onshore partnership that uses leverage can generate unrelated business taxable income.
cards.originalText: All capital is pooled and all trading occurs in the master fund, which is funded by multiple feeder vehicles designed for different investor groups; typically one feeder serves onshore investors and another serves offshore investors, with the offshore feeder generally used for non-U.S. investors and for U.S. tax-exempt investors such as pension funds. The structure avoids multiple layers of taxation and allows tax-exempt investors to participate tax-efficiently.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: In a hedge fund master-feeder structure, trading occurs separately within each feeder to give investor groups differentiated exposure, and the master fund exists solely as an administrative consolidation vehicle for reporting.
cards.explanation: In a master-feeder structure all capital is pooled and all trading occurs in the master fund. The feeders exist to accommodate different investor groups, mainly for tax reasons.
cards.originalText: Trading occurs separately within each feeder to give investor groups differentiated exposure, and the master fund exists solely as an administrative consolidation vehicle for reporting.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: In a U.S.-domiciled hedge fund's master-feeder structure, all capital is pooled in the master fund, and the offshore feeder is used exclusively for non-U.S. investors, since U.S. tax-exempt investors are required to invest through the onshore feeder.
cards.explanation: The offshore feeder is generally used both by non-U.S. investors and by U.S. tax-exempt investors such as pension funds, allowing the latter to participate tax-efficiently.
cards.originalText: All capital is pooled in the master fund, and the offshore feeder is used exclusively for non-U.S. investors, since U.S. tax-exempt investors are required to invest through the onshore feeder.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: A hedge fund master-feeder structure exists primarily to allow the manager to charge different fee levels to different investor groups, and its tax consequences are incidental.
cards.explanation: Tax efficiency is the stated purpose of the master-feeder structure: it avoids multiple layers of taxation and allows tax-exempt investors to participate tax-efficiently.
cards.originalText: The structure exists primarily to allow the manager to charge different fee levels to different investor groups, and its tax consequences are incidental.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: In the United States, Delaware is a common domicile because of its favourable legal environment; offshore funds are most frequently located in the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands and Bermuda, in that order of prevalence.
cards.explanation: Delaware is the common onshore U.S. choice. Offshore, the Cayman Islands hosts about 55% of funds, the British Virgin Islands about 15% and Bermuda about 10%.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: Hedge funds require accountants, lawyers, auditors, administrators and independent valuation professionals to determine net asset value, and rely on a prime broker for lending, counterparty services, trade execution, clearing and settlement.
cards.explanation: Hedge funds depend on a network of service providers. The prime broker provides lending, acts as counterparty and handles execution, clearing and settlement.
cards.originalText: Funds require accountants, lawyers, auditors, administrators and independent valuation professionals to determine net asset value, and rely on a prime broker for lending, counterparty services, trade execution, clearing and settlement.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: Hedge fund domicile is chosen to minimise taxes and reduce regulatory oversight, and because the choice eliminates tax at every level, neither the manager's fees nor the investors' gains attract tax once an offshore domicile is used.
cards.explanation: An offshore domicile can reduce tax at the fund level, but managers still pay tax on the fees they earn and investors remain taxable on their gains in their home jurisdictions.
cards.originalText: Domicile is chosen to minimise taxes and reduce regulatory oversight, and because the choice eliminates tax at every level, neither the manager's fees nor the investors' gains attract tax once an offshore domicile is used.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure
cards.statement: Valuation performed by the fund administrator is generally regarded as more independent than valuation performed by the fund manager.
cards.explanation: The manager has an incentive to flatter reported values, so valuation by a third-party administrator is regarded as more independent and more reliable.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private investment vehicles require less expertise from investors than public markets.
cards.explanation: Private markets require more expertise, not less. Direct private investing in particular demands significant expertise and active involvement.
cards.originalText: require less expertise from investors.
cards.correction: Private investment vehicles require more expertise from investors than public markets.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private investment vehicles require more expertise from investors than public markets.
cards.explanation: Private markets require more expertise, not less. Direct private investing in particular demands significant expertise and active involvement.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private investment vehicles harness the power of home country bias.
cards.explanation: One benefit of private investment vehicles is that they can help reduce home country bias by giving access to opportunities beyond the investor's domestic public market.
cards.originalText: harness the power of home country bias.
cards.correction: Private investment vehicles help reduce home country bias.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private investment vehicles help reduce home country bias.
cards.explanation: One benefit of private investment vehicles is that they can help reduce home country bias by giving access to opportunities beyond the investor's domestic public market.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private investment vehicles guarantee higher returns than public markets.
cards.explanation: No investment guarantees higher returns. Investors may seek higher returns in private markets, but those returns come with illiquidity and other risks.
cards.originalText: guarantee higher returns than in public markets.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private investment vehicles offer investors greater control over the value creation process.
cards.explanation: Private investors can monitor, guide and influence company performance, a level of control generally unavailable in public markets without a very large stake, and they contribute capital, connections and operational expertise.
cards.originalText: offer investors greater control over the value creation process.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private equity can be structured as common or preferred shares, with preferred shares negotiable to include specific rights and protections so that not all preferred shares offer the same features; private debt can be convertible or nonconvertible with senior, subordinate or junior rights, and convertible debt provides downside protection through its debt component and upside potential through the conversion option.
cards.explanation: Private preferred shares are negotiated deal by deal, unlike standardised public preferred stock. Private debt comes in varying seniority, and a convertible combines a protective debt component with an upside conversion feature.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private equity can be structured as common or preferred shares, and preferred shares carry a standardised set of rights across the market, which is what makes them comparable between deals.
cards.explanation: Private preferred shares are negotiated to include specific rights and protections, so their features differ from deal to deal and are not standardised.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Private debt is always structured as senior secured obligations, since the absence of a public market makes subordinated private lending uninvestable.
cards.explanation: Private debt can carry senior, subordinate or junior rights, each with different priority over other creditors, and it can be convertible or nonconvertible.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics
cards.statement: Convertible private debt provides upside potential through its debt component and downside protection through the conversion option, which is why it is preferred in distressed situations.
cards.explanation: The two components are reversed. The debt component of a convertible provides downside protection, and the right to convert into equity provides upside potential.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: The denominator effect, a form of valuation risk in private markets, arises when an outdated private asset valuation is compared with the value of a highly liquid public asset, leading to distorted comparisons; because the resulting weight difference may be artificial, it can lead to unnecessary rebalancing.
cards.explanation: Private assets transact infrequently, so their marks go stale. After a public selloff the private weight can rise purely because total portfolio value has fallen, and rebalancing on that artificial deviation would be unnecessary.
cards.originalText: Valuation risk, specifically the denominator effect, where an outdated private asset valuation is compared with the value of a highly liquid public asset, leading to distorted comparisons; because the resulting weight difference may be artificial, it can lead to unnecessary rebalancing.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: Selection risk reflects the possibility of choosing the wrong manager or deal, and it is not symmetrical because the performance of top managers can differ substantially from that of bottom performers; the wide dispersion between the top 5% and bottom 5% also creates challenges for Monte Carlo simulations.
cards.explanation: Manager dispersion in private markets is wide and skewed, far more than in public equity funds. That asymmetry makes manager selection a first-order decision and makes outcomes hard to simulate with standard distributional assumptions.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: Selection risk is symmetrical around the median manager, which is what allows a normal distribution to be assumed in Monte Carlo simulation of private market outcomes.
cards.explanation: Selection risk in private markets is not symmetrical: top managers can differ substantially from bottom performers. The wide dispersion between the top and bottom 5% is what makes Monte Carlo simulation challenging.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: Selection risk reflects the possibility of choosing the wrong manager, and it can be eliminated entirely by allocating to a fund of funds, since diversification across managers removes idiosyncratic manager risk.
cards.explanation: A fund of funds reduces selection risk by diversifying across managers, but it cannot eliminate it. It adds another layer of fees and creates a selection decision of its own: which fund of funds to choose.
cards.correction: Selection risk reflects the possibility of choosing the wrong manager, and it can be reduced by allocating to a fund of funds, since diversification across managers reduces idiosyncratic manager risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: Selection risk reflects the possibility of choosing the wrong manager, and it can be reduced by allocating to a fund of funds, since diversification across managers reduces idiosyncratic manager risk.
cards.explanation: A fund of funds reduces selection risk by diversifying across managers, but it cannot eliminate it. It adds another layer of fees and creates a selection decision of its own: which fund of funds to choose.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: Selection risk arises only in private equity and not in private debt, because private debt returns are contractually specified and therefore do not depend on manager skill.
cards.explanation: Private debt outcomes also depend on manager skill, notably the ability to limit recovery losses, so selection risk applies to private debt as well as private equity.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
cards.statement: In private markets, SAA risk arises when a long-term allocation deviates from a market-neutral benchmark, with investability and access constraints limiting the ability to hold the target; TAA risk is associated with market timing, is harder in private markets because a commitment made today may not deploy for several years, and is mitigated by time diversification across vintage years over a 5 to 7 year period.
cards.explanation: Strategic asset allocation risk concerns long-term deviation from a market-neutral benchmark; tactical asset allocation risk concerns market timing. The lag between commitment and deployment makes timing hard in private markets, so investors spread commitments across vintage years.
