cards.statement: For a distressed firm, complexity is a limitation because a layered capital structure gives the firm more options than a simple one, which makes selecting among them harder and delays execution.
cards.explanation: A layered capital structure gives a distressed firm fewer choices, not more, because restrictive covenants and consent requirements, especially from secured bank lenders, close off remedies.
cards.originalText: Complexity is a limitation because a layered capital structure gives the firm more options than a simple one, which makes selecting among them harder and delays execution.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method
cards.statement: Severability favours firms with only core operations, since a single integrated business can be sold whole at a premium, whereas a conglomerate must dispose of units piecemeal at a discount.
cards.explanation: Severability favours firms with noncore units, which can be sold to reduce leverage without harming the core business. Firms with only core operations lack that flexibility.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: The holdout problem arises when nonparticipating creditors believe they may receive better terms than those who cooperate, and if too many hold out the restructuring may fail and trigger a costly bankruptcy leaving everyone worse off; it is addressed through the implied threat of future economic leverage, since major distressed investors interact across multiple deals, and through coercive mechanisms such as a tender offer that amends the bonds of nonparticipants to remove protective covenants once the majority accepts, or an exchange offer combined with a request to support a prepackaged bankruptcy.
cards.explanation: Out-of-court restructurings are voluntary, so holdouts cannot be compelled. Repeated-game reputation effects and coercive structures such as exit consents stripping covenants, or a prepackaged bankruptcy backstop, reduce the incentive to hold out.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: The holdout problem arises because nonparticipating creditors are legally bound by a majority vote in an out-of-court restructuring, and it is addressed by increasing the majority threshold required for approval.
cards.explanation: Holdouts exist precisely because participation in an out-of-court restructuring is voluntary and nonparticipants are not bound. Raising an approval threshold would make holding out more powerful, not less.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: The holdout problem is confined to bank debt, since bond indentures already permit a simple majority to bind all holders to any amendment.
cards.explanation: The debt types are reversed. Bank debt amendments can often bind lenders by majority, whereas bonds are where holdouts arise and coercive tools such as exit consents are needed.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: The holdout problem is addressed principally by the indenture trustee, who has authority to accept restructuring terms on behalf of all bondholders without seeking their consent.
cards.explanation: The indenture trustee is the formal representative of the bondholders but generally seeks broad consensus among them before acting, to minimise legal risk. It does not unilaterally accept restructuring terms.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: In Chapter 11, claimants are grouped into classes based on similar characteristics and common interests, and all members of a class must receive the same treatment; the typical classes in order are administrative claims, super secured claims representing debtor-in-possession financing, priority claims for pre-petition employee obligations, super secured claims of pre-petition secured lenders, senior unsecured claims of trade creditors and unsecured noteholders, and equity.
cards.explanation: The reorganisation plan must treat every member of a class equally. DIP financing is given priority to make lending to an insolvent borrower possible, and equity sits last.
cards.originalText: Claimants are grouped into classes based on similar characteristics and common interests, and all members of a class must receive the same treatment; the typical classes in order are administrative claims, super secured claims representing debtor-in-possession financing, priority claims for pre-petition employee obligations, super secured claims of pre-petition secured lenders, senior unsecured claims of trade creditors and unsecured noteholders, and equity.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: In Chapter 11, debtor-in-possession financing ranks behind pre-petition secured lenders, since existing security interests cannot be primed by post-petition lending.
cards.explanation: Debtor-in-possession financing receives super secured priority over pre-petition secured lenders and other claims; that priming is what makes DIP lending available to an insolvent borrower.
cards.originalText: Claimants are grouped into classes, and debtor-in-possession financing ranks behind pre-petition secured lenders, since existing security interests cannot be primed by post-petition lending.
cards.correction: In Chapter 11, debtor-in-possession financing ranks ahead of pre-petition secured lenders, since existing security interests can be primed by post-petition lending.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: In Chapter 11, debtor-in-possession financing ranks ahead of pre-petition secured lenders, since existing security interests can be primed by post-petition lending.
cards.explanation: Debtor-in-possession financing receives super secured priority over pre-petition secured lenders and other claims; that priming is what makes DIP lending available to an insolvent borrower.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: In Chapter 11, members of the same class may receive different treatment where the debtor negotiates individually, which is what makes a plan confirmable.
cards.explanation: All members of a class must receive the same treatment. Classes are formed from claimants with similar characteristics and common interests precisely to prevent individual deals within a class.
cards.originalText: Claimants are grouped into classes, and members of the same class may receive different treatment where the debtor negotiates individually, which is what makes a plan confirmable.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: In Chapter 11, pre-petition employee obligations rank behind senior unsecured trade creditors, since employees have recourse to statutory wage protection schemes and therefore do not require priority within the plan.
cards.explanation: Pre-petition employee obligations are priority claims ranking ahead of senior unsecured trade creditors and noteholders.
cards.originalText: Pre-petition employee obligations rank behind senior unsecured trade creditors, since employees have recourse to statutory wage protection schemes and therefore do not require priority within the plan.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: Debt can be restructured either with or without court supervision; court-supervised restructurings can be time-consuming, costly and damaging to a firm's reputation, while an out-of-court restructuring depends on voluntary participation and can therefore be undermined by holdouts.
cards.explanation: Each route has its own drawback. In-court proceedings bind dissenters but are slow, expensive and reputationally damaging; out-of-court deals avoid those costs but cannot compel holdouts.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: Out-of-court restructurings are generally slower and more expensive than in-court proceedings, because the absence of a statutory framework requires each term to be negotiated individually with every creditor.
cards.explanation: It is court-supervised restructurings that tend to be time-consuming, costly and damaging to reputation. The main weakness of out-of-court restructurings is vulnerability to holdouts.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: In-court restructuring is available only after an out-of-court attempt has formally failed, since the bankruptcy court will not accept a petition from a firm that has not exhausted consensual alternatives.
cards.explanation: There is no such precondition. A prepackaged bankruptcy, for example, is a filing made with a consensual deal already agreed.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Summarize potential legal challenges that can arise when a firm is in financial distress or is going through a restructuring
cards.statement: A firm entering Chapter 11 has no strategic discretion over the timing or jurisdiction of its filing, since both are determined by the location of its principal place of business and the date of its first payment default.
cards.explanation: Both the timing and the jurisdiction of a Chapter 11 filing involve strategic considerations for the firm.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: An equity market neutral strategy targets zero net market exposure so that returns derive from security selection rather than direction, whereas a long/short equity strategy typically maintains a net long bias and therefore retains meaningful market exposure.
cards.explanation: Market neutral is defined by the constraint that net market exposure is approximately zero. Long/short equity has no such constraint and usually runs net long, so part of its return is market beta.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: An equity market neutral strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas a long/short equity strategy targets zero net exposure by construction.
cards.explanation: The profiles are reversed. Equity market neutral targets approximately zero net exposure, while long/short equity typically runs a net long bias.
cards.correction: A long/short equity strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas an equity market neutral strategy targets zero net exposure by construction.

changes.from: An equity market neutral strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas a long/short equity strategy
changes.to: A long/short equity strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas an equity market neutral strategy

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A long/short equity strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas an equity market neutral strategy targets zero net exposure by construction.
cards.explanation: The profiles are reversed. Equity market neutral targets approximately zero net exposure, while long/short equity typically runs a net long bias.

changes.from: An equity market neutral strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas a long/short equity strategy
changes.to: A long/short equity strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas an equity market neutral strategy

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Equity market neutral and long/short equity strategies both target zero net market exposure, and they differ only in the holding period of the underlying positions.
cards.explanation: Only equity market neutral targets zero net exposure. Long/short equity typically maintains a net long bias, and holding period is not what distinguishes them.
cards.originalText: Both strategies target zero net market exposure, and they differ only in the holding period of the underlying positions.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A global macro strategy is a form of equity market neutral strategy, since macro managers hedge all directional exposure through index futures.
cards.explanation: Global macro is directional by design, taking leveraged positions on macroeconomic developments across currencies, rates, commodities and equity indices.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A convertible bond position delta-hedged by shorting the underlying equity is long volatility, since the embedded conversion option gains value as realised volatility rises, and the delta hedge removes first-order directional exposure while leaving the convexity of the option intact.
cards.explanation: A convertible is debt plus a long equity call. Shorting delta shares removes first-order price sensitivity but not the embedded call's convexity (gamma), so the hedged position profits from realised volatility. It also retains credit exposure to the issuer.
cards.originalText: The position is long volatility, since the embedded conversion option gains value as realised volatility rises, and the delta hedge removes first-order directional exposure while leaving the convexity of the option intact.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A convertible bond position delta-hedged by shorting the underlying equity is short volatility, since writing the equity short is equivalent to selling an option on the underlying.
cards.explanation: A short stock position is linear and carries no optionality. The long embedded call in the convertible makes the hedged position long volatility.
cards.originalText: The position is short volatility, since writing the equity short is equivalent to selling an option on the underlying.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A convertible bond position delta-hedged by shorting the underlying equity is directionally neutral and volatility neutral, which is why convertible arbitrage returns are uncorrelated with all market factors.
cards.explanation: The delta-hedged position is long volatility and retains credit and liquidity exposure. Convertible arbitrage performed very badly in 2008 precisely because of those exposures.
cards.originalText: The position is directionally neutral and volatility neutral, which is why convertible arbitrage returns are uncorrelated with all market factors.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A convertible bond position delta-hedged by shorting the underlying equity is long credit risk only, since delta-hedging removes both the equity and the volatility exposure, leaving the issuer's default risk as the sole driver.
cards.explanation: Delta hedging removes first-order equity exposure but not gamma, so the position remains long volatility as well as exposed to the issuer's credit risk.
cards.originalText: The position is long credit risk only, since delta-hedging removes both the equity and the volatility exposure, leaving the issuer's default risk as the sole driver.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A merger arbitrage strategy earns a small, high-probability spread if the deal completes and suffers a large loss if it breaks, producing a return profile resembling a written put and therefore negative skewness.
cards.explanation: If the deal closes the arbitrageur captures the spread; if it breaks the target typically falls back toward its pre-announcement price. Many small gains and occasional large losses is the payoff shape of a written put.
cards.originalText: The strategy earns a small, high-probability spread if the deal completes and suffers a large loss if it breaks, producing a return profile resembling a written put and therefore negative skewness.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A merger arbitrage strategy earns a large payoff on completion and loses a small premium if the deal breaks, producing positive skewness comparable to a long option position.
cards.explanation: The asymmetry is the reverse: a small spread on completion and a large loss on a break, which resembles a written put and produces negative skewness.
cards.originalText: The strategy earns a large payoff on completion and loses a small premium if the deal breaks, producing positive skewness comparable to a long option position.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: A merger arbitrage strategy is genuinely market neutral in all states, since the long target and short acquirer positions offset regardless of whether the deal completes.
cards.explanation: The hedge holds only while the deal is live. If the deal breaks, the target and acquirer prices move apart and the position suffers a large loss.
cards.originalText: The strategy is genuinely market neutral in all states, since the long target and short acquirer positions offset regardless of whether the deal completes.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: In merger arbitrage, deal completion probability is the only determinant of expected return, so the target's pre-announcement price is not required to evaluate the trade.
cards.explanation: The target's pre-announcement price determines the loss if the deal fails, so expected return depends on the completion probability, the gain on completion, the loss on failure, the current price and the time to completion.
cards.originalText: Deal completion probability is the only determinant of expected return, so the target's pre-announcement price is not required to evaluate the trade.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The fulcrum security is the most junior claim in the structure, since junior claims offer the greatest upside in a successful reorganisation.
cards.explanation: The most junior claim, usually equity, is generally wiped out. The fulcrum security is the most senior claim expected to be only partially repaid, and it is typically converted into the reorganised firm's equity.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: The fulcrum security is identified from the coupon rate, with the highest-coupon instrument being the fulcrum because it carries the greatest cash burden on the issuer.
cards.explanation: The fulcrum is determined by position in the capital structure and by enterprise value: it is where the value runs out. Coupon rate is irrelevant.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations
cards.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
cards.statement: Distressed investing carries no valuation risk once a Chapter 11 petition is filed, since claim priority is fixed by statute and recoveries follow mechanically.
cards.explanation: Claim priority is fixed, but enterprise value is not. The valuation determines where impairment falls, so a lower-than-expected value can impair a claim that looked safe.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds
cards.statement: A lockup prevents redemption for a stated initial period; a gate limits the proportion of fund or investor capital that may be redeemed in any single period; and a side pocket segregates specific illiquid holdings so that they are realised only when the underlying asset is sold.
cards.explanation: Lockups prevent early withdrawal, gates slow outflows to avoid forced selling in a run, and side pockets stop redeeming investors from taking the liquid assets and leaving illiquid holdings to those who remain.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds
cards.statement: A gate prevents redemption for a stated initial period, and a lockup limits the proportion redeemable in any period.
cards.explanation: The definitions are swapped. A lockup prevents redemption for an initial period; a gate caps the proportion of capital that can be redeemed in any single period.
cards.correction: A lockup prevents redemption for a stated initial period, and a gate limits the proportion redeemable in any period.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds
cards.statement: A lockup prevents redemption for a stated initial period, and a gate limits the proportion redeemable in any period.
cards.explanation: The definitions are swapped. A lockup prevents redemption for an initial period; a gate caps the proportion of capital that can be redeemed in any single period.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds
cards.statement: A side pocket is a temporary suspension of all redemptions imposed by the regulator during a market stress event.
cards.explanation: A side pocket is a manager-operated segregation of specific illiquid holdings, realised only when those assets are sold. It is not a regulatory suspension.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds
cards.statement: Lockups, gates and side pockets apply only to offshore feeder vehicles, since onshore partnerships must offer redemption on demand.
cards.explanation: Lockups, gates and side pockets are contractual terms set in the partnership agreement and can apply to both onshore and offshore vehicles.
cards.originalText: All three restrictions apply only to offshore feeder vehicles, since onshore partnerships must offer redemption on demand.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk
cards.statement: Hedge fund activity can transmit stress to the wider financial system through leverage obtained from prime brokers, which links fund losses directly to bank balance sheets; through crowded positioning, so that simultaneous unwinding by similarly positioned funds amplifies price moves; and through forced deleveraging, where margin calls compel sales that depress prices and trigger further calls.
cards.explanation: All three channels operated at LTCM. That is why the financial-stability objective of hedge fund regulation focuses on limiting leverage and requiring timely and accurate posting of collateral.
cards.originalText: Through leverage obtained from prime brokers, which links fund losses directly to bank balance sheets; through crowded positioning, so that simultaneous unwinding by similarly positioned funds amplifies price moves; and through forced deleveraging, where margin calls compel sales that depress prices and trigger further calls.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk
cards.statement: Hedge funds transmit stress to the wider financial system principally through the size of the industry's assets under management, since systemic importance is determined by absolute scale rather than by interconnection or leverage.
cards.explanation: Systemic risk from hedge funds comes mainly from leverage, counterparty linkages, crowding and forced deleveraging. LTCM was modest in assets but systemically dangerous because of its leverage and connections.
cards.originalText: Principally through the size of the industry's assets under management, since systemic importance is determined by absolute scale rather than by interconnection or leverage.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk
cards.statement: Hedge funds cannot transmit systemic stress, since losses fall on sophisticated investors who have accepted the risk and no public money is at stake.
cards.explanation: Hedge funds can transmit stress through prime broker leverage, crowded trades and forced deleveraging, as LTCM showed. That is why Dodd-Frank requires hedge fund advisers to report to the SEC and FSOC.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk
cards.statement: Hedge funds transmit stress to the wider financial system through their obligation to publish position-level disclosures, which allows other market participants to trade against them during periods of stress.
cards.explanation: Hedge funds do not publish position-level disclosures; Form PF is filed confidentially with regulators. Stress transmits through leverage, crowding and forced deleveraging.
cards.originalText: Through their obligation to publish position-level disclosures, which allows other market participants to trade against them during periods of stress.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of private credit, including its typical investors and borrowers
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit loans are typically bilateral or club deals held to maturity by a small number of lenders, are largely floating rate, are not traded and therefore not marked to market by observable prices, and are extended predominantly to middle-market firms often owned by private equity sponsors.
cards.explanation: Unlike broadly syndicated loans and high-yield bonds, private credit has no secondary market with observable prices and is valued by model or appraisal. It lends mainly to middle-market, often sponsor-backed, borrowers at floating rates.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of private credit, including its typical investors and borrowers
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit loans trade in a liquid secondary market comparable to broadly syndicated loans, which is what allows daily valuation.
cards.explanation: Private credit loans are generally not traded and are held to maturity. The absence of a secondary market is a defining feature and the source of valuation concerns.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of private credit, including its typical investors and borrowers
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit borrowers are predominantly large investment-grade corporates seeking to avoid public disclosure obligations.
cards.explanation: Private credit borrowers are predominantly middle-market firms, often owned by private equity sponsors and typically below investment grade.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of private credit, including its typical investors and borrowers
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit is predominantly fixed rate, which is why the asset class benefited from the rate rises of 2022 and 2023.
cards.explanation: Private credit is largely floating rate. Rising rates increased borrowers' debt-service burdens, which was a source of stress rather than a benefit.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit valuations are infrequent and appraisal based rather than market based, which smooths reported returns and understates true volatility and correlation with public markets; the return premium reflects compensation for illiquidity and credit risk rather than a free lunch.
cards.explanation: Stale appraisal-based values produce autocorrelated reported returns, suppressing measured volatility, beta and correlation without reducing actual risk. A mean-variance optimiser fed smoothed inputs would over-allocate to private credit.
cards.originalText: Valuations are infrequent and appraisal based rather than market based, which smooths reported returns and understates true volatility and correlation with public markets; the return premium reflects compensation for illiquidity and credit risk rather than a free lunch.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit managers hedge interest rate and credit spread risk more effectively than public market investors, which genuinely reduces the volatility of the asset class.
cards.explanation: Private credit is largely unhedged floating-rate lending to leveraged borrowers. Its low reported volatility comes from infrequent, appraisal-based valuation that smooths returns.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Private credit exhibits genuinely low correlation with public credit because the borrowers are unlisted and therefore unaffected by public market conditions.
cards.explanation: Being unlisted affects how returns are observed, not the underlying exposure. Middle-market borrowers are highly sensitive to the same macro conditions, and smoothed valuations understate the true correlation.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: The lower reported volatility of private credit reflects the shorter duration of private credit loans, which mechanically reduces mark-to-market variation.
cards.explanation: Private credit loans are not marked to market by observable prices at all. The low reported volatility is a smoothing artefact of infrequent, appraisal-based valuation, not a duration effect.
cards.originalText: The lower reported volatility reflects the shorter duration of private credit loans, which mechanically reduces mark-to-market variation.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Deteriorating credit quality and looser underwriting as competition for deals intensifies, including a rising incidence of payment-in-kind arrangements that defer cash interest, are a vulnerability of the private credit market.
cards.explanation: Intensifying competition for deals has loosened underwriting, and growing use of payment-in-kind interest can mask borrower stress. Credit quality deterioration is one of the recognised private credit vulnerabilities.
cards.originalText: Deteriorating credit quality and looser underwriting as competition for deals intensifies, including a rising incidence of payment-in-kind arrangements that defer cash interest.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Layered leverage, where leverage exists at the borrower, the fund and the investor level simultaneously, so that a shock is amplified at each layer, is a vulnerability of the private credit market.
cards.explanation: Leverage stacked at the borrower, fund and investor levels means a single shock is amplified at each layer, which is one of the recognised private credit vulnerabilities.
cards.originalText: Layered leverage, where leverage exists at the borrower, the fund and the investor level simultaneously, so that a shock is amplified at each layer.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: Opacity and stale valuations, which delay recognition of losses and make aggregate exposures difficult for supervisors to observe, are a vulnerability of the private credit market.
cards.explanation: Because private credit is not traded, losses are recognised late and supervisors struggle to see aggregate exposures. Opacity is one of the recognised private credit vulnerabilities.
cards.originalText: Opacity and stale valuations, which delay recognition of losses and make aggregate exposures difficult for supervisors to observe.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: The private credit market is characterised by daily redemption terms across the asset class, which create an immediate liquidity mismatch between redeemable liabilities and illiquid loan assets.
cards.explanation: Private credit is dominated by closed-end funds with locked capital, which makes it less run-prone than open-ended bond funds. The liquidity concern is the growth of semi-liquid vehicles offering periodic redemption, not market-wide daily redemption.
cards.originalText: Daily redemption terms across the asset class, which create an immediate liquidity mismatch between redeemable liabilities and illiquid loan assets.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: The recommended policy direction for private credit is a more intrusive supervisory approach centred on closing data gaps through enhanced reporting, monitoring leverage and interconnections across banks, insurers and funds, strengthening liquidity and conduct requirements where retail participation is growing, and improving valuation and stress-testing practices.
cards.explanation: Supervisors cannot yet see aggregate private credit exposures, so the recommendation starts with data and visibility rather than capital, followed by monitoring of leverage and interconnection, targeted retail safeguards and better valuation and stress testing.
cards.originalText: A more intrusive supervisory approach centred on closing data gaps through enhanced reporting, monitoring leverage and interconnections across banks, insurers and funds, strengthening liquidity and conduct requirements where retail participation is growing, and improving valuation and stress-testing practices.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: The recommended policy direction for private credit is extending the bank capital framework to private credit funds so that they hold risk-weighted capital against loan exposures on the same basis as banks.
cards.explanation: The recommendations focus on supervision, reporting, liquidity and conduct requirements, and valuation and stress testing, not on imposing bank-style risk-weighted capital on funds.
cards.originalText: Extending the bank capital framework to private credit funds so that they hold risk-weighted capital against loan exposures on the same basis as banks.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: The recommended policy direction for private credit is prohibiting retail access entirely, since the liquidity mismatch cannot be managed through disclosure or structural requirements.
cards.explanation: The recommendation is to strengthen liquidity and conduct safeguards where retail participation is growing, not to prohibit retail access.
cards.originalText: Prohibiting retail access to private credit entirely, since the liquidity mismatch cannot be managed through disclosure or structural requirements.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit
cards.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
cards.statement: The recommended policy direction for private credit is deferring supervisory action until a credit event materialises, since the absence of realised losses indicates that current arrangements are adequate.
cards.explanation: The concern is precisely that private credit has not been tested through a full default cycle, so the recommendation is for more intrusive supervision now, not waiting for losses.
cards.originalText: Deferring supervisory action until a credit event materialises, since the absence of realised losses indicates that current arrangements are adequate.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets
cards.statement: The potential for higher returns, including an illiquidity premium, is a motivation for investing in private markets.
cards.explanation: Higher return potential, including compensation for giving up liquidity, is one of the stated motivations for private market investing.
cards.originalText: The potential for higher returns, including an illiquidity premium.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets
cards.statement: Greater control over the value creation process, through monitoring, guiding and influencing company performance, is a motivation for investing in private markets.
cards.explanation: Private investors can monitor, guide and influence company performance to a degree generally unavailable in public markets, which is one of the stated motivations.
cards.originalText: Greater control over the value creation process, through monitoring, guiding and influencing company performance.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets
cards.statement: Wider geographic and sector reach, including exposure to regions where public markets are underdeveloped, which helps reduce home country bias, is a motivation for investing in private markets.
cards.explanation: Private markets give access to regions, sectors and companies that public markets do not reach, which helps diversify and reduce home country bias.
cards.originalText: Wider geographic and sector reach, including exposure to regions where public markets are underdeveloped, which helps reduce home country bias.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets
cards.statement: Improved portfolio liquidity is a motivation for investing in private markets, since private funds offer redemption terms negotiated to match the investor's liability profile.
cards.explanation: Liquidity is what an investor gives up to access private markets; the illiquidity premium is the compensation for that sacrifice. Improved liquidity is not a motivation.
cards.originalText: Improved portfolio liquidity, since private funds offer redemption terms negotiated to match the investor's liability profile.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Studies of historical hedge fund failures find that a majority are attributable to operational issues, including misrepresentation of investments, misappropriation of funds, unauthorised trading and inadequate resources, rather than investment losses alone.
cards.explanation: Investment losses are a real cause of failure but not the majority one. That finding is why operational due diligence deserves heavy weight in hedge fund selection.
cards.originalText: Operational issues, including misrepresentation of investments, misappropriation of funds, unauthorised trading and inadequate resources, rather than investment losses alone.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Studies of historical hedge fund failures find that a majority are attributable to investment losses arising from adverse market movements, which is why market risk measurement is the primary focus of hedge fund due diligence.
cards.explanation: Studies find that a majority of hedge fund failures stem from operational issues such as misrepresentation, misappropriation, unauthorised trading and inadequate resources, so due diligence should weight operations heavily.
cards.originalText: Investment losses arising from adverse market movements, which is why market risk measurement is the primary focus of hedge fund due diligence.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Studies of historical hedge fund failures find that a majority are attributable to regulatory enforcement action, which forces closure before losses can be realised by investors.
cards.explanation: A majority of hedge fund failures are attributable to operational issues. Enforcement action typically follows a failure rather than causing it.
cards.originalText: Regulatory enforcement action, which forces closure before losses can be realised by investors.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
cards.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
cards.statement: Studies of historical hedge fund failures find that a majority are attributable to redemption pressure alone, independent of any operational or investment failure.
cards.explanation: A majority of hedge fund failures are attributable to operational issues. Redemption pressure is a business model risk and is usually a symptom of a prior problem.
cards.originalText: Redemption pressure alone, independent of any operational or investment failure.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress
cards.statement: The trading level of a distressed firm's debt reflects the current market price of that debt relative to its full repayment value and serves as an indicator of the market's expectations about distress severity and the range of potential restructuring solutions, so the level itself helps narrow which remedies are realistic.
cards.explanation: Where debt is actively traded, a modest discount is consistent with a liquidity problem solvable by refinancing or asset sales, while a deep discount signals an expected balance-sheet restructuring with principal written down.
cards.originalText: The trading level reflects the current market price of the firm's debt relative to its full repayment value and serves as an indicator of the market's expectations about distress severity and the range of potential restructuring solutions, so the level itself helps narrow which remedies are realistic.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress
cards.statement: The trading level of a distressed firm's debt reflects only prevailing interest rates, so a discount indicates a rate move rather than any change in the firm's credit condition.
cards.explanation: For a distressed firm the credit component dominates the debt's price. The trading level signals the market's view of distress severity and likely restructuring outcomes.
cards.originalText: The trading level reflects only prevailing interest rates, so a discount indicates a rate move rather than any change in the firm's credit condition.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress
cards.statement: A debt trading level below par indicates that bankruptcy is unavoidable, since the market has already determined that creditors will not be repaid in full.
cards.explanation: A discount to par is consistent with several outcomes, including an out-of-court restructuring. The trading level helps distinguish among possible solutions rather than determining a single one.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress
cards.statement: Debt trading levels are unusable for distressed analysis because private credit and bank debt do not trade, so no observable price exists for any distressed issuer.
cards.explanation: The trading-level approach applies wherever a firm's debt is actively traded. Lack of prices for some private debt is a real limitation, but it does not apply to every distressed issuer.
cards.originalText: The trading level is unusable for distressed analysis because private credit and bank debt do not trade, so no observable price exists for any distressed issuer.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Madoff reported using a split-strike conversion, holding a basket of large-cap equities while buying puts and selling calls to bracket the return; the results were implausible because the strategy produced remarkably consistent positive returns with almost no down months, whereas a split-strike conversion should track equity markets and lose money when they fall sharply.
cards.explanation: A collar is correlated with the equity market: the put limits losses but does not eliminate them. Smooth positive returns through severe equity declines were inconsistent with the stated strategy.
cards.originalText: A split-strike conversion, holding a basket of large-cap equities while buying puts and selling calls to bracket the return; the results were implausible because the strategy produced remarkably consistent positive returns with almost no down months, whereas a split-strike conversion should track equity markets and lose money when they fall sharply.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Madoff reported using a global macro strategy trading currencies and rates through derivatives, whose returns were implausible because macro strategies cannot produce positive returns in trending markets.
cards.explanation: Madoff reported a split-strike conversion (a collar on large-cap equities). Macro strategies also typically perform well, not badly, in trending markets.
cards.originalText: A global macro strategy trading currencies and rates through derivatives, whose returns were implausible because macro strategies cannot produce positive returns in trending markets.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: Madoff reported using a convertible arbitrage strategy whose returns were implausible because convertible arbitrage cannot generate positive returns without leverage.
cards.explanation: Madoff reported a split-strike conversion, not convertible arbitrage, and convertible arbitrage can generate positive returns without leverage.
cards.originalText: A convertible arbitrage strategy whose returns were implausible because convertible arbitrage cannot generate positive returns without leverage.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential red flags
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: The most significant operational red flag at Madoff's firm was the absence of an independent third-party administrator and custodian, with the firm performing execution, custody, administration and valuation itself, and using a three-person audit firm for a purported multi-billion dollar operation.
cards.explanation: Self-custody and self-administration removed every independent check at once: no third party held the assets, valued them or confirmed the trades. The tiny audit firm had no capacity to audit an operation of the claimed size.
cards.originalText: The absence of an independent third-party administrator and custodian, with the firm performing execution, custody, administration and valuation itself, and using a three-person audit firm for a purported multi-billion dollar operation.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential red flags
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: The most significant operational red flag at Madoff's firm was its use of a large, well-known prime broker, which created concentration risk in a single counterparty.
cards.explanation: There was no independent prime broker or custodian: Madoff's firm executed, held and valued the assets itself, which removed every independent check.
cards.originalText: The fund's use of a large, well-known prime broker, which created concentration risk in a single counterparty.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential red flags
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: The most significant operational red flag at Madoff's firm was its high headline fee structure, which was well above industry norms and should have prompted questions about value for money.
cards.explanation: Madoff charged no management or performance fee on the advisory business, taking only purported commissions. The key operational red flag was self-custody and self-administration with a tiny audit firm.
cards.originalText: The fund's high headline fee structure, which was well above industry norms and should have prompted questions about value for money.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential red flags
cards.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
cards.statement: The most significant operational red flag at Madoff's firm was its frequent public marketing, which breached the private placement restrictions under Regulation D.
cards.explanation: Madoff's marketing relied on exclusivity rather than publicity. The key operational red flag was the lack of an independent administrator and custodian, together with a tiny audit firm.
cards.originalText: The fund's frequent public marketing, which breached the private placement restrictions under Regulation D.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario approach, shocks are applied to a small subset of K policy risk drivers, typically major traded instruments such as an equity index, bond yields or factor-mimicking portfolios, and the shocks to the remaining M minus K nonpolicy factors are implied through multivariate regression to generate the full perturbation vector; keeping the number of policy variables small helps minimise arbitrariness in the resulting vector.
cards.explanation: MDS is a conditional framework: experts shock a few well-understood policy variables and the rest are implied from the covariance structure. Each extra policy variable is another judgement call, so a small policy set limits arbitrariness.
cards.originalText: Shocks are applied to a small subset of K policy risk drivers, typically major traded instruments such as an equity index, bond yields or factor-mimicking portfolios, and the shocks to the remaining M minus K nonpolicy factors are implied through multivariate regression to generate the full perturbation vector; keeping the number of policy variables small helps minimise arbitrariness in the resulting vector.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario approach, shocks are specified independently for all M risk factors by expert judgment, and the covariance structure is used afterwards to check internal consistency.
cards.explanation: MDS shocks only a small set of policy variables by judgement; the shocks to the remaining nonpolicy factors are implied by regression on the covariance structure.
cards.originalText: Shocks are specified independently for all M risk factors by expert judgment, and the covariance structure is used afterwards to check internal consistency.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: In the market-driven scenario approach, shocks are applied to as many policy variables as possible, since a larger policy set produces a more precisely specified perturbation vector and reduces arbitrariness.
cards.explanation: The design principle is the reverse: keep the number of policy variables small, because each additional one is another judgement call and increases arbitrariness.
cards.originalText: Shocks are applied to as many policy variables as possible, since a larger policy set produces a more precisely specified perturbation vector and reduces arbitrariness.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach applies a uniform percentage shock across all risk factors, with correlations ignored so that the resulting scenario is conservative.
cards.explanation: MDS shocks a small set of policy variables and uses the covariance structure to imply the remaining shocks. Ignoring correlations is the opposite of the method and does not reliably produce a conservative scenario.
cards.originalText: The approach applies a uniform percentage shock across all risk factors, with correlations ignored so that the resulting scenario is conservative.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance
cards.statement: The Mahalanobis distance is a multivariate generalisation of a z-score using the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables; the scenario z-score rescales it so that it does not increase in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables, and when comparing two scenarios the one with the lower scenario z-score is more plausible; the volatility z-score isolates the magnitude component by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero; and the correlation z-score normalises the scenario z-score for shock magnitude.
cards.explanation: These four measures form the MDS plausibility toolkit: the Mahalanobis distance measures outlier-ness, the scenario z-score rescales it for the number of variables, and the volatility and correlation z-scores split it into magnitude and co-movement components.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance
cards.statement: The scenario z-score measures plausibility such that a higher score indicates a more plausible scenario, since a higher score reflects greater consistency with the historical covariance structure.
cards.explanation: A higher scenario z-score indicates a more severe, less plausible scenario. When comparing two scenarios, the one with the lower scenario z-score is more plausible.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance
cards.statement: The volatility z-score isolates the correlation component by holding shock magnitudes constant, and the correlation z-score isolates the magnitude component by setting all correlations to zero.
cards.explanation: The components are swapped. The volatility z-score isolates magnitude by setting all correlations to zero; the correlation z-score normalises the scenario z-score for magnitude to isolate co-movement consistency.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance
cards.statement: The Mahalanobis distance uses the covariance matrix directly rather than its inverse, which is what allows it to be interpreted in standard deviation units.
cards.explanation: The Mahalanobis distance uses the inverse covariance matrix, which is what standardises the distance so it can be read in standard deviation units, accounting for correlations.
cards.correction: The Mahalanobis distance uses the inverse covariance matrix rather than the covariance matrix directly, which is what allows it to be interpreted in standard deviation units.

changes.from: the covariance matrix directly rather than its inverse
changes.to: the inverse covariance matrix rather than the covariance matrix directly

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance
cards.statement: The Mahalanobis distance uses the inverse covariance matrix rather than the covariance matrix directly, which is what allows it to be interpreted in standard deviation units.
cards.explanation: The Mahalanobis distance uses the inverse covariance matrix, which is what standardises the distance so it can be read in standard deviation units, accounting for correlations.

changes.from: the covariance matrix directly rather than its inverse
changes.to: the inverse covariance matrix rather than the covariance matrix directly

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios
cards.statement: In developing a market-driven scenario, the sequence is to define the narrative and identify the policy variables it implies; specify the shocks to those policy variables; assess the plausibility of the proposed shock vector using the scenario z-score and the risk ruler; derive the implied shocks to nonpolicy factors by regression; then compute portfolio impact, fully revaluing positions with nonlinear payoffs.
cards.explanation: The narrative determines the relevant policy variables, and plausibility is checked before effort is spent propagating shocks. Nonpolicy shocks are implied last, and positions with optionality are fully revalued rather than approximated.
cards.originalText: Define the narrative and identify the policy variables it implies; specify the shocks to those policy variables; assess the plausibility of the proposed shock vector using the scenario z-score and the risk ruler; derive the implied shocks to nonpolicy factors by regression; then compute portfolio impact, fully revaluing positions with nonlinear payoffs.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios
cards.statement: In developing a market-driven scenario, the portfolio impact is computed first across a wide range of arbitrary shocks, and the shock vector producing the largest loss is then selected and a narrative constructed to justify it.
cards.explanation: That describes reverse stress testing. A market-driven scenario starts from a narrative, specifies policy shocks, checks plausibility, implies other shocks by regression and only then computes portfolio impact.
cards.originalText: Compute the portfolio impact first across a wide range of arbitrary shocks, then select the shock vector producing the largest loss and construct a narrative to justify it.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios
cards.statement: In developing a market-driven scenario, the implied nonpolicy shocks are derived first and policy variable shocks are then chosen to be consistent with them, since the nonpolicy factors are more numerous and therefore more informative.
cards.explanation: The conditional structure runs the other way: policy variable shocks are specified first and the nonpolicy shocks are outputs implied from them by regression.
cards.originalText: Derive the implied nonpolicy shocks first, then choose policy variable shocks consistent with them, since the nonpolicy factors are more numerous and therefore more informative.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios
cards.statement: In developing a market-driven scenario, shocks to all factors should be specified simultaneously by expert judgment, since regression-implied shocks embed historical relationships that may not hold under stress.
cards.explanation: MDS specifies shocks only for a small set of policy variables and implies the rest by regression. The instability of historical relationships under stress is a recognised challenge, not a reason to abandon the regression step.
cards.originalText: Specify shocks to all factors simultaneously by expert judgment, since regression-implied shocks embed historical relationships that may not hold under stress.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges and considerations that may arise when implementing the market-driven scenario approach
cards.statement: The most significant challenge in implementing the market-driven scenario approach is that the implied shocks depend entirely on the estimated covariance matrix, so the choice of estimation window determines the result: a long history embeds regimes no longer relevant, while a short recent window may omit the stress relationships the scenario is designed to capture, and correlations themselves change under stress.
cards.explanation: Everything downstream of the policy shocks comes from the estimated covariance structure, so its estimation is the dominant model risk. Correlations typically rise in stress, so a calm-period matrix understates crisis co-movement.
cards.originalText: The implied shocks depend entirely on the estimated covariance matrix, so the choice of estimation window determines the result: a long history embeds regimes no longer relevant, while a short recent window may omit the stress relationships the scenario is designed to capture, and correlations themselves change under stress.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges and considerations that may arise when implementing the market-driven scenario approach
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach requires the full perturbation vector to be specified by expert judgment, which makes it prohibitively labour intensive for large portfolios.
cards.explanation: Only a small set of policy variables is specified by judgement; shocks to all other factors are implied by regression.
cards.originalText: The approach requires the full perturbation vector to be specified by expert judgment, which makes it prohibitively labour intensive for large portfolios.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges and considerations that may arise when implementing the market-driven scenario approach
cards.statement: The market-driven scenario approach cannot accommodate positions with nonlinear payoffs, since portfolio impact is computed as a linear function of factor shocks.
cards.explanation: Positions with nonlinear payoffs are fully revalued using the perturbation vector, so MDS can accommodate optionality.
cards.originalText: The approach cannot accommodate positions with nonlinear payoffs, since portfolio impact is computed as a linear function of factor shocks.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges and considerations that may arise when implementing the market-driven scenario approach
cards.statement: Scenario z-scores translate directly into absolute probabilities without further assumptions, which gives users false confidence in the precision of the estimates.
cards.explanation: Scenario z-scores measure relative plausibility. Converting them into absolute probabilities requires additional parametric or nonparametric assumptions.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices for managing liquidity risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Liquidity risk management should be independent of portfolio management, integrated across the investment process from pre-trade through ongoing monitoring, supported by governance with clear escalation, and calibrated to both the liquidity of the assets and the redemption profile of the liabilities.
cards.explanation: A fund's liquidity risk is the interaction of asset liquidity with redemption terms. Best practice combines independence, integration across the investment process, governance with escalation, and calibration to both sides of the balance sheet.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices for managing liquidity risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Liquidity risk should be owned by the portfolio management team, since they hold the most detailed knowledge of the positions and can act fastest.
cards.explanation: Liquidity risk management should be independent of portfolio management. Portfolio managers have an interest in how their positions' liquidity is assessed, and knowledge is not the same as independence.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices for managing liquidity risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Liquidity risk management should focus on the asset side alone, since redemption behaviour is driven by investors and cannot be modelled.
cards.explanation: Liquidity risk management must cover both asset liquidity and the redemption profile of the liabilities, and redemption behaviour can be modelled.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices for managing liquidity risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Liquidity should be assessed at the point of purchase only, since a security's liquidity characteristics are established at issuance and do not change materially.
cards.explanation: Liquidity varies materially with market conditions, so it must be monitored on an ongoing basis, not just assessed at purchase.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios
cards.statement: Liquidity modelling is more difficult for corporate bonds than for listed equities because bonds trade over the counter and infrequently, so volume data is sparse and price discovery is poor; a single issuer may have many outstanding lines with different liquidity; and reported volume understates potential capacity, the difference being latent liquidity.
cards.explanation: Sparse OTC trading, many different lines per issuer and the gap between observed volume and potential capacity all complicate bond liquidity models. Latent liquidity can be estimated using tail measures of the ADV distribution.
cards.originalText: Bonds trade over the counter and infrequently, so volume data is sparse and price discovery is poor; a single issuer may have many outstanding lines with different liquidity; and reported volume understates potential capacity, the difference being latent liquidity.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios
cards.statement: Corporate bond trading is fully reported in real time with no size caps, so the difficulty in modelling bond liquidity arises from an excess of data rather than a shortage.
cards.explanation: Corporate bonds trade over the counter and often sporadically, so data is sparse. Trade reporting also carries size caps that mask the largest trades.
cards.originalText: Corporate bond trading is fully reported in real time with no size caps, so the difficulty arises from an excess of data rather than a shortage.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios
cards.statement: Corporate bonds trade on exchanges with continuous order books, so the challenge in modelling their liquidity is one of interpreting depth rather than of missing observations.
cards.explanation: Corporate bonds trade predominantly over the counter without continuous order books, and many trade infrequently, so observations are often missing.
cards.originalText: Corporate bonds trade on exchanges with continuous order books, so the challenge is one of interpreting depth rather than of missing observations.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios
cards.statement: Bond liquidity is stable through time, so a single historical estimate suffices and the challenge in modelling it is purely computational.
cards.explanation: Bond liquidity varies substantially through time, and daily volume is highly variable, so a single historical estimate is not sufficient.
cards.originalText: Bond liquidity is stable through time, so a single historical estimate suffices and the challenge is purely computational.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests
cards.statement: Suspension of redemptions, permitted where continued dealing would prejudice remaining investors and typically requiring regulatory notification or approval, is an extraordinary measure a regulator may permit a fund to use in meeting unanticipated redemptions.
cards.explanation: Suspension is one of the extraordinary redemption measures, alongside redemption in kind, side pockets, gates, temporary borrowing and swing pricing or anti-dilution levies. It usually requires regulatory notification or approval.
cards.originalText: Suspension of redemptions, permitted where continued dealing would prejudice remaining investors, typically requiring regulatory notification or approval.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests
cards.statement: Redemption in kind, transferring a pro rata slice of portfolio securities to the redeeming investor instead of cash, is an extraordinary measure a regulator may permit a fund to use in meeting unanticipated redemptions.
cards.explanation: Redemption in kind hands securities rather than cash to the exiting investor, so the fund avoids selling those holdings and the exiting investor does not impose liquidation costs on those who remain.
cards.originalText: Redemption in kind, transferring a pro rata slice of portfolio securities to the redeeming investor instead of cash.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests
cards.statement: Side pockets or the segregation of illiquid assets, and temporary borrowing to bridge a redemption where permitted by the fund's terms, are extraordinary measures a regulator may permit a fund to use in meeting unanticipated redemptions.
cards.explanation: Side pockets ring-fence illiquid holdings, and temporary borrowing buys time for orderly sales. Both are among the recognised extraordinary redemption measures where the fund's terms and regime allow them.
cards.originalText: Side pockets or the segregation of illiquid assets, and temporary borrowing to bridge a redemption where permitted by the fund's terms.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests
cards.statement: Selling the most illiquid assets first to preserve the liquidity of the remaining portfolio is the standard first response to unanticipated redemptions before any extraordinary measure is sought.
cards.explanation: A fund meeting redemptions normally works from cash and the most liquid assets first, then progressively less liquid holdings. Selling the most illiquid assets first would realise the worst prices at the worst time.
cards.originalText: Selling the most illiquid assets first to preserve the liquidity of the remaining portfolio, which is the standard first response before any extraordinary measure is sought.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Redemption-at-risk estimates a high percentile of the distribution of net outflows over a horizon, analogous to value at risk applied to the liability side, using historical redemption data segmented by investor type since institutional, retail and intermediated flows behave differently; the redemption waterfall then determines the order in which assets are liquidated to meet it.
cards.explanation: Redemption-at-risk is a VaR-style tail measure for liabilities. Segmentation matters because retail, institutional and platform money redeem very differently, and the waterfall then sets the liquidation order.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Redemption-at-risk uses the mean of historical net flows, since extreme percentiles are unreliable in a series with few observations.
cards.explanation: Redemption-at-risk is a high percentile of the net outflow distribution. A mean cannot measure the tail outflow the measure exists to capture.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund
cards.statement: Redemption modelling should treat all investors as a single homogeneous group, since segmenting by investor type introduces estimation error without improving accuracy.
cards.explanation: Segmenting by investor type is essential, because institutional, retail and intermediated investors redeem very differently and concentration in the investor base is itself a risk.

cards.subject: Investment Risk
cards.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund
